speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to a number of questions from hon. members I would like to make a progress report on arrangements under the Canada Student Loans Act. I have delayed doing so pending receipt of information from the provinces on whether they are participating in the plan and on the arrangements they are making to get the plan under way.
All provinces, the Yukon and Northwest Territories have now decided to participate in this plan, except the province of Quebec. As all hon. members knew at the time the legislation was before the house, the province of Quebec was intending to continue to rely entirely on its own comprehensive plan of student loans, bursaries and scholarships.
Appropriate authorities, as provided under the act, are designated by the provinces as the authority in the province for the purposes of the Canada students loans plan. Nine provinces and the two territories have provided us informally with the following names and addresses of the appropriate authorities which they are designating for this purpose. I will not read the addresses, but in most cases the address is in care of the department of education:
Newfoundland
Prince Edward Island Nova Scotia
New Brunswick
Ontario
Manitoba

Alberta
British Columbia

Except in the case of Ontario, these appropriate authorities will be the only agencies in the province to which students should apply for certificates of eligibility. These certificates may be issued to students who meet the provincial standards on academic qualifications and financial need.
In Ontario, all universities and other specified educational institutions will be entitled to issue certificates of eligibility to students. These institutions are listed in the appendix to this statement. By leave of the house I should like to suggest that this statement be printed as an appendix to Hansard, but if hon. members feel this would not be appropriate it could be done in some other way. However, I think it would be convenient to have the whole matter dealt with in the same document.

Ontario students applying for a certificate in connection with studies abroad must apply to the Ontario department of university affairs.
All the forms which we must provide in order that the plan may get under way will be sent out next Monday, August 31, to all appropriate authorities of the provinces and to the banks across the country. Regulations under the Canada Student Loans Act will be published in the Canada Gazette during the first week of September.
A brochure is being prepared which will tell students about the qualifications necessary to apply for certificates of eligibility and loans, how much they can borrow, how long they can take to repay, what the cost is likely to be and, most important, where they should apply in each province. This brochure will be printed and available next week for distribution in large numbers to the banks and,

Inquiries of the Ministry through the provincial authorities, to universities and other educational institutions. Copies of this brochure will be distributed to members of parliament.
Thanks to the wholehearted co-operation of all concerned, the Canada student loans plan will be launched, as promised, before the beginning of the academic year 1964-65. In this connection I should like to express the appreciation of the government to all the provinces, without exception, for their ready and helpful participation in our discussions, sometimes at short notice and at no small personal inconvenience to those involved.
Officials of the chartered banks have also co-operated in this endeavour and the government is grateful to them. May I also express a special word of thanks to the officials of several federal departments, including my own, who have worked under very heavy pressure to put this plan into effect at the earliest possible date.

speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of Justice. The question relates to a tape recording of a radio interview between Ed Murphy and Cowlishaw and Macdonald in which Macdonald said that unless some action is taken by three o'clock today he intends to go across the country and "blow the lid off" the R.C.M.P. security system. Yesterday the minister said he would investigate this case. Has he done so, and is he in a position to make a statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORTED CLAIM OF FORMER AGENT
speechtext:
My answer was given in reply to a question asking whether I was investigating the case. It is obvious that in my capacity as Minister of Justice it is my obligation to do so. But the question whether the facts as alleged by either Mr. Cowlishaw or Mr. Macdonald are accurate is a totally different one, and I think I can only answer it in the words of a previous minister of justice in a former administration, words which I think are absolutely right and which I want to make my own. These are the words of Hon. Davie Fulton in answer to a question asked in the House of Commons on April 29, 1959, as reported in Hansard of that year at page 3152. I will take full responsibility for them today:
I can only answer the question by saying that the government has consistently followed a policy of complete reticence concerning security work, which in such a case means that it must refuse either to acknowledge or deny allegations about the employment of secret sources for intelligence work.
I repeat that under my own responsibility I make those words of Mr. Fulton my own.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORTED CLAIM OF FORMER AGENT
speechtext:
supplementary question, following the answer given to my hon. friend from Danforth. I should like to ask the Minister of Justice

whether he would not agree that if it is true that a man is being discriminated against because of an association with the communist party which he undertook on behalf of the
R.C.M.P., the government and in particular the Minister of Justice has a responsibility to clear this man's name in the circumstances?
Can I ask the minister if he accepts this principle and whether he is prepared to look into the matter on this basis? It seems to me it is not sufficient to tell us that a previous minister of justice said he must be reticent on this subject. If this man's statement is true, his good name is at stake. Surely the minister has the responsibility to clear his good name if the facts he gave to the public are correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORTED CLAIM OF FORMER AGENT
speechtext: Evidently the question is predicated on an assumption. Therefore it is hypothetical. Second, it purports to ask for a personal opinion on my part. I must tell the house that the answer which was given by a previous minister of justice and which I adopted as my own is the same as was given by ministers of justice in still earlier administrations. This represents an attitude which in certain cases, I must admit, makes for certain apparent hardships. However, it is important and essential to the security of the whole of Canada that as far as these matters are concerned the same line of conduct be followed by this government as was followed by previous governments.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORTED CLAIM OF FORMER AGENT
speechtext: Would not the minister be as interested in the security of this individual, whose livelihood is affected, as he would be in the security of the R.C.M.P.? If he has had an unfortunate association at the request of the R.C.M.P., and paid for by the R.C.M.P., surely his name should be cleared.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF REPORTED CLAIM OF FORMER AGENT
speechtext: Of course I never did refer, and I never would, to the security of the R.C.M.P. as such. This is a gallant body, each of whose members will always place his personal safety and security at the disposal of Canada. I was referring to the security of the whole of Canada, the country as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege which I would have raised at the start of today's proceedings but the Leader of the Opposition, who is involved in it, was a few seconds late in getting into the house. That is quite understandable, but I did not want to raise it until he was in his place. I might also have raised it yesterday when the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg raised his point of privilege about a statement which appeared in Time, but as far as my question of privilege is concerned, it was not until this morning that I obtained the necessary transcript so as to be sure of the words used which I feel need correction.
I happened to hear the voice of the Leader of the Opposition over radio station CKPM here in Ottawa the night before last and again yesterday morning, when he made a statement in which there were two errors which should be corrected. I have obtained a transcript from Mr. Paul Taylor of CKPM, and I should like to read the words which I think should be corrected. At one point, referring to my open letter of August 12 to the party leaders, the Leader of the Opposition said:
When I received his open letter, which was first given to the press-
-and so on. I wish to make it clear, so that all hon. members may know the facts, that I delivered copies of my open letter by hand-not through a messenger; I delivered them myself-to the office of each leader between nine o'clock and five minutes after nine o'clock on Wednesday morning, August 12. I personally delivered copies to the press later for release at eleven o'clock that morning. That is the first correction.

Canadian Flag
The other statement in the transcript I have in my hand arises out of the reference made by the Leader of the Opposition to the occasion when he offered to place my name before the house in nomination for the speakership of this house. He used these words:
For some reason known to him he refused to allow his name to go before the house-
The implication there is that I did not give my reasons. The Leader of the Opposition knows that I wrote him on August 24, 1957, setting out the reasons for my refusal. My letter was in reply to his letter of August 19, 1957, in which he made the offer; and he, the Leader of the Opposition, who was then prime minister, tabled both these letters in the House of Commons on October 17, 1957. They comprise sessional paper No. 178 of that session.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that nothing tremendous turns on these two misstatements, but it is my view that statements made in public by public men should be in accord with the facts.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I would call attention to the fact that the debate was adjourned last night by the Minister without Portfolio, and we should hear from him now.
If he has anything to say.
I understand that the Chair did not recognize him last night, although I notice that according to Hansard he did ask that it be declared six o'clock.
He must be out selling stickers.

Mr. Speaker, last night the Minister without Portfolio called it six o'clock, but evidently the hon. member's business has now become so important that he has not even time to stay in this house and complete his speech. We have always been looking for a label for the hon. gentleman, and I suggest we now call him the "minister of bumper stickers".
This letter which he sent to his colleagues is quite interesting and should be brought to the attention of this house. I have a photostat of the letter, which I should like to put on record. It says:
My dear Colleague:
If you are interested, I can procure-

Order. I do not like interrupting the hon. member, but a copy of this letter has been tabled today and is available to any hon. member who wishes to see it. We have had considerable discussion about it. Perhaps the hon. member would confine himself to the subamendment.

On a point of order, this letter is referring to the subamendment because it deals with the three maple leaves flag which the hon. member is trying to advertise across this country. It is time some of this propaganda was brought to the attention of the Canadian people. This letter has to do with the three maple leaves flag and goes on to say:
-I can procure at a very special price: $25 per thousand stickers.. .of the proposed flag.
Order.

I believe that every member should sell at least 1,000 to the most important service stations In his riding. The garage manager could then distribute them to each client who buys at his station.
Thus, the result would be better (and would look less political) than if the member undertook this publicity himself.
In my riding I have already placed 12 orders of 1,000 in the gas stations of 12 different localities.
For information or orders call Mr. Gordon Marshall 992-2237. (Only those orders of 1,000 decals or more will be accepted).
The hon. member told his colleagues that he had a special price of $25 per thousand for the proposed maple leaf bumper stickers. I became very interested in this subject this morning and made a number of phone calls. I found one place where I could buy them for $21 per thousand. Where is the extra money going? Is that extra money going to be put in the Liberal campaign fund? Is that party going to benefit in this way by pushing a proposed flag down our throats? I think the situation is disgraceful. I suggest the Prime Minister and his cabinet are engaging in a propaganda campaign in respect of this flag. If the Prime Minister walked into this chamber now and withdrew his motion and placed the flag issue before a committee I would be glad to take my seat. If he does not do so I shall continue to speak on this resolution at this time, and perhaps speak again on four or five other occasions.
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate the second time I feel I am doing so with great responsibility. I am supporting the retention of the red ensign or a slightly modified red ensign. Canada has prospered for 96 years under the red ensign. The people of Canada have lived together happily, and we have witnessed intermarriage among the French, English, Ukrainians and many other nationalities. I suggest there is no excuse for the Prime Minister or anyone else at this time to cause the dissension across this country that is now being caused.
Mr. Speaker, I have a resolution before me which I should like to read. This resolution states:
Whereas the red ensign as the flag of Canada, is the symbol of:
(1)	democracy,
(2)	parliamentary government,
(3)	justice and tolerance,
(4)	freedom of the individual,
(5)	freedom of worship,
(6)	educational opportunity for all,
Canadian Flag
(7)	initiative and industry,
and whereas, under this flag and these principles Canada has been developed, and whereas, the red ensign was chosen as the flag of Canada by authority of an order in council September 5, 1945, by the government of Canada, and whereas, it was the flag used by the Canadian forces in the last two wars, and now in Cyprus and also carried by the Canadian teams in the Olympic games,
Mr. Speaker, I am expressing the feelings of millions of people in this country when I speak in support of the red ensign. Statistics indicate that nine of the ten provinces in this great country of ours support the red ensign as Canada's national flag. I am sure the people in that other province would also accept the red ensign were it not for the brainwashing which has been done by extremists and university professors, such as we see sitting in the cabinet across from us today.
Mr. Speaker, we in the Conservative party are being accused of filibustering. Let me say that we are not filibustering but fighting on behalf of the people in Canada who support the retention of the red ensign. The members of this party seem to stand alone in this house on this flag issue. We do not have the support of the members of the party to our left. I have a great deal of respect for the leader of the New Democratic party. I know he comes from a part of this country which is in support of the red ensign. That part of the country is not receiving much support from the N.D.P. members in this house.
What has happened to that great parliamentarian, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who likes to hear himself, even though he must resort to phony points of privilege in order to put his remarks on record? I am sure his constituents are going to be unhappy about his position in this matter.
What has happened to that great Social Credit party next to us? I give the hon. member for Fraser Valley and the hon. member for Cariboo credit for at least rising in their places in this house and taking a stand. What have the rest of the members of that party done?
What has that great parliamentarian, the hon. member for Red Deer, had to say about the flag issue? Mr. Speaker, I have a Time magazine bearing the date August 28, 1964 before me. I suggest that it is in Time magazine that that hon. gentleman takes a position. He makes his position known outside this house. According to that article Bob Thompson, for one, is fed up. I have received a letter from a Social Credit supporter in

Mr. Speaker, that is a downright lie. I belong to that party, and we discussed this issue at each and every one of our caucuses. The hon. member for Red Deer should not make statements of that type across this country which are, as I repeat, downright lies. That hon. gentleman has contributed nothing to this debate. Why is he not here?
My remarks would apply in respect of any hon. member, for that matter.

Mr. Speaker I submit that is not a point of order. I am referring to that which appeared in a newspaper, sir. If an hon. member is not here it is not my responsibility. The only sensible remark that has been made by a member of that party during this flag debate was made the night before last by the hon. member for Portneuf, who suggested that before individuals be allowed to stand for election they should be given I.Q. tests. I doubt very much that the hon. members over there would stand up to the I.Q. test.
You would never get back.

If you want to make a speech go across the river and make it.
Mr. Speaker, let us hear from those members on the Liberal side of this house. We

would like to hear from the Ontario members. We have heard from the hon. member for York-Humber and the hon. member for York East, who at least got up on their feet and expressed their opinions. The rest of those hon. members have sat quiet.
The Prime Minister, as a result of poor advice, has placed before this parliament the three maple leaves design flag, as mentioned in the subamendment and the resolution. This flag is not acceptable across this country. Why was the Prime Minister in such a hurry to place this flag resolution before this parliament? Surely there is a great deal more important business that should be dealt with by this house. The hon. member for York-Humber told us that this design was not placed before them in that party, or mentioned in their caucus, but was brought in in a hurry shortly after the Minister of Forestry attended the Quebec conference. Does this flag resolution have something to do with the government's proposed pension plan?
Mr. Speaker, I suggest the flag issue represents one of the biggest blunders that any prime minister has made. He now finds himself with little support for his flag across this country. I suggest he should now give further consideration to this whole matter. He has suggested that the design proposed could not be mistaken for the flag of any other country.
He stated that our present flag is too much like the British merchant flag, and we should get away from that. On several occasions I have mentioned that I have looked through the flag book. I am not allowed to display this, but if anyone cares to come to my desk and look at this flag he will find that the Russian naval flag closely resembles the one proposed by the Prime Minister. It has a white fly, the hammer, sickle and star in red, and a blue band on the bottom. Are we going to throw out our red ensign because it looks like the British merchant flag and accept a flag with the colours of the Russian naval flag? No; we are going to put up a big fight before we have to accept this.
I wonder why the Prime Minister fell for these colours. When we asked for the tabling of the correspondence referring to the flag we found this letter, which says that the communist party supports the proposal for a new Canadian flag. I will not read all this letter but it also says "We urge you to reject the proposal for a plebiscite." I am going to leave this thought with you today, fellow members in this chamber and fellow Canadians across

this country. Think about these statements that have been put on the record today. If you doubt my word, get a flag book and take a look at that Russian naval flag. Then there is that communication. I am going to tell you today that if something is not done about this flag, if we are going to have this flag forced down our throats, then the next speech I make will be one in which I will put a lot more documents on the record and there will be some people with red faces before we are through.
After?

You did enough yapping yesterday. If you just sit on your seat and keep your brains warm you will be a lot better off. Nothing has split this country more than this flag issue. This process was started under the B and B commission, and now we have the flag issue to add to it. As stated by the hon. member for York-Humber earlier, there was no mention of the flag anywhere but in the province of Quebec. Out west we were offered $2 wheat, and I suppose in the maritimes they were offered a larger amount for fish or lumber. The people of Quebec resent the fact that they are being used as tools for political purposes. I have talked to many people from the province of Quebec. The French Canadians are fine people, and I have a great many friends amongst them. I have been through the province of Quebec, and when you get to the rural areas you find the farming people very friendly. They would like to see this government do something for them. They cannot eat a flag, but they could do with some assistance to agriculture. The Minister of Agriculture has not the legislation prepared yet, so we have to fight over this flag.
Only the other night several good French Canadians told me they were being embarrassed by the actions of these intellectuals, these Creditistes and the people who are speaking about the desire for this new flag. Quebec has a fleur-de-lis flag. Premier Lesage says this new flag will be their second flag.
What about the third one?
Well, the Prime Minister will give them a third one, too.
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. Could the hon. member tell the house where verification can be found for his statement about Premier Lesage? Was the statement made to him?

That is no question of privilege.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-
We already have one question of privilege.
That is a phony point of order; he is usually yapping on these points of order.
This is a point of order. A member of this house is required to substantiate any declaration he has made by giving the source of that declaration.

If you had to substantiate your thoughts or declarations you would have a hard time, because you do not have any thoughts. I said I wanted to speak in support of the red ensign. I should like to place on record a portion of an open letter to the Prime Minister from Winnipeg:
Dear Sir:
Mr. Pearson, in his latest speech on the "Nation's Business", stressed two points: 1, the need for Canadian unity-2, the need for a "distinctive" Canadian flag.
Regarding the first point, i.e. the need for Canadian unity, everybody knows that the public controversy aroused to date by the introduction of Mr. Pearson's flag has reduced Canadian unity to the lowest ebb in our history.
Regarding the second point, i.e. the need for a "distinctive" Canadian flag, only Mr. Pearson seems to be unaware of the fact that we have in the red ensign one of the most distinctive flags in the world. Where it flies on Canadian embassies, no one fails to recognize it as Canadian. Only Mr. Pearson seems to doubt this. Yet Mr. Pearson's flag possesses no distinctiveness whatsoever, and can in no way be compared with our nation's flag, the Canadian red ensign.
I would say to hon. members here today that if they consider we do not have a distinctive flag they should go over to the front of the west block, walk up and down and look at the flags displayed there. They will see that the Canadian flag stands out from all the others that are there.
Here is a letter now to Right Hon. John Diefenbaker:
Dear Mr. Diefenbaker:
We have been greatly encouraged by your last pronouncement on the "Nation's Business" on television regarding the flag issue, and also by the news report that your party is continuing the fight for the red ensign.
The loss of the red ensign would cause a split in our nation such as we have never known before. This split added to the Pearson bicultural rift could spell the ruination of our future as a nation.
We believe that if the people of Canada fully understood the traditions represented by the symbols on the red ensign, they would overwhelmingly endorse its retention as our flag.
You and your party are our last hope for preserving unity. We, therefore, thank you for your continuing efforts on behalf of the great majority of Canadians.

Canadian Flag
These are the reasons, Mr. Speaker, for our support of this flag. There are more letters that I could read, but I see my time is nearly exhausted. I say, sir, this matter is becoming serious. Something must be done. The government got itself into this problem by trying to force the maple leaf flag on the Canadian people when they are not prepared to accept it. The next move is up to the Prime Minister. I am reminded of the old proverb which says he who is on the wrong track and will not turn back is a fool. I say to the government, you are on the wrong track and it is time you turned back and withdrew this resolution. You should accept the recommendation for a committee or a plebiscite or some means of letting the Canadian people choose the distinctive flag they want.
We hear a lot about our flag not being distinctive and not being known throughout the world, but I have a picture here of our soldiers over in France and the red ensign is flying as they march by. The time has come for the government to give very serious consideration to withdrawing the flag resolution. The Prime Minister will be looked upon across Canada with a great deal more respect than he is today if he does that, because people will know he has realized he made a mistake and is man enough to acknowledge it.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

No member may speak twice to a question except in explanation of a material part of his speech which may have been misquoted or misunderstood-
I understand he will be very brief, and that it is in the nature of a correction.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. That is what I desire to do, to take brief advantage of the opportunity presented by standing order 37. Yesterday during the debate on this matter the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, as recorded at page 7304 of Hansard, made the following statement:
I was also interested in the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) the other day. Everybody in the house knows he is a very active Anglican layman, and I say more power to him. But in his speech he disowned completely the

red ensign and its historic traditions and connections with the Anglican church. He made absolutely no reference to it. I am not criticizing his stand but I think he should have tried to explain this change in his thinking.
In the very brief contribution I did make to this debate a few days ago I did not disown the red ensign. In fact, on the contrary I specifically proposed that the red ensign be officially recognized as a symbol in Canada of the commonwealth. But what is a lot more important is the statement by the hon. member that I disowned the historic connection of the Anglican church with the red ensign.
So far as I know the Anglican church at no time has taken any stand whatsoever on what would be a suitable flag for Canada, and has no historic connection with the red ensign. There is no such thing as Anglican orthodoxy on this issue and the hon. member, as an Anglican, has just as much right to his view as I, another Anglican, have to disagree with him. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have only one or two more sentences. I would like to remind hon. members in this house-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I rise on a point of order. This, I understand, is a point of privilege which the hon. member is raising?

Both the hon. member and I did not think it was important enough to raise right at the opening of the sitting, and I suggested to him that inasmuch as it concerned the flag debate he could ask the indulgence of the house for two or three minutes to correct what he believed was a misinterpretation of his statements.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It seems a bit odd to me that rebuttal of statements made in the course of debate should be done by way of privilege on this occasion. Surely the hon. member can participate again and deal with any remarks made in the course of debate here by way of rebuttal. All he is doing now is smuggling in a rebuttal by way of a question of privilege. I think this is quite wrong. If it is to be the established practice of the house, then it is open to all members to do the same on any occasion when something is said with which they disagree. The hon. member should take his opportunity in the debate, and there will be other opportunities for him to make a rebuttal.

The last part of standing order 37(1) says:
-but then he is not to introduce any new matter, and no debate shall be allowed upon such explanation.

I was interrupted for a moment, but I understood the non. member was trying to explain a material part of his speech which may have been misconstrued or misunderstood, and I am sure if the hon. member would stick to that we would have no more trouble.

I just have one or two more things to say, and that is what I was trying to do, to say I was misunderstood by the hon. member who said I had somehow or other abandoned Anglican tradition. I was about to finish my remarks by pointing out that the Anglican church of Canada itself, when it adopted its own flag or emblem, which I believe was approved by statute in this house, had incorporated in its emblem not one, not three, but in fact four maple leaves, coloured green, not red, and they were not conjoined. But there is no Anglican tradition that requires people of loyalty to the Anglican church to adopt any particular flag, and I deplore my hon. friend interjecting into this debate the reference to some supposed religious orthodoxy on the matter before the house.
The particular church we are both discussing has broadened out so that the old jibe is no longer true, that the Anglican church was the Tory party at prayer. I do not think we should have that suggestion.

With great respect, Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of order. The hon. gentleman knows very well that type of statement has no place whatsoever after he has participated in debate. While interested, as one of Baptist persuasion always is in questions of ecclesiastical orthodoxy, I do not think even that fact justifies what the hon. gentleman has done.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate because I believe the concern I feel is shared literally by millions of Canadians. My concern is for something more than the various flags we are discussing; my concern is for parliament itself.
I dearly wish it were possible for some kind of mirror to be installed so that all of us in this parliament could see what it looks like during the course of this debate. If we cannot do that at least I feel we should pay some attention to the reports we are getting from our people back home, the pleadings that are reaching us that we discipline ourselves to the point of reaching a decision on the matters that are now before us.

Last Saturday I had the privilege of spending the day in a lovely rural town in my own province of Manitoba. On that day I was not in my own constituency; I was in the constituency of my friend the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns). It is an area that is Conservative. My purpose in rising is to urge all of us in this house to take a very close look at ourselves and at what we are doing by this protracted debate, and by the character of the debate at times-people can read Hansard for this afternoon-to the institution of parliament itself. I plead with all my friends in the house in all parties, whatever may be their views on the flag, to realize that there is something more important than winning this debate, winning an issue, or seeing that one leader triumphs over the other. That more important goal is to maintain the dignity and the integrity and the importance of parliament itself. Hon. members know that I am a strong advocate of-

-finding ways and means of disciplining ourselves so that we do not have protracted debates. that enough of us will be opposed to the application of closure. I ask them not to continue with the kind of protracted debate which can do nothing but bring parliament into discredit and disgrace in the eyes of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

and that is that we are abdicating our responsibilities as the elected parliament of Canada. I plead with hon. members of this house to realize what we are doing, by the way in which we are carrying on this debate. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that any effort to impose any kind of closure on this debate will meet with my opposition. I ask hon. members not to confuse that with the efforts I am making regarding future debates; but I say that so far as this debate is concerned closure must not be applied to it. Would the hon. member not agree that when the government or the executive pursues an arbitrary and a divisive course in its policy, the only recourse of the legislature is a continuation of discussion; and is this not the course that his party pursued in connection with divorce matters?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Some members of my party pursued that course with respect to that matter.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Just a minute. Don't get so excited; I didn't come to parliament yesterday. This whole party took that position with respect to the pipe line debate in 1956. As my hon. friend knows, what he has said is right in principle, and I will assert it; that if a government is trying to do something that members feel is completely inimical to everything the nation stands for-
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
-yes, those who take that position should use what weapons they have at their disposal to try and prevent that happening. But I say two things to them. They must be sure they are right in the stand they take; and the other thing is that they must also remember there is such a thing as the right of a parliamentary body to make a decision.
My hon. friends of the Conservative opposition keep talking about the minority government ramming something down their throats. May I say to them that by their continuing this debate they are preventing a decision being taken; they are preventing our being given an opportunity to move an amendment for a single maple leaf, as they know we wish to do; they are preventing proper parliamentary procedures; they are preventing parliament from making a decision; they are preventing us from getting at other business; they are preventing us from running the country; they are turning things over to the establishment.
Hear, hear.
Now we see the plot.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who has just taken his seat-

Canadian Flag

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am sorry; I have not taken my seat.
Well, I am on a point of order.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: All right.

The hon. member said that because this debate is being prolonged the government is being prevented from dealing with other business. It is my understanding, as it is his, that the Prime Minister of this country said that as soon as this debate was over we were going to take a recess. If the Conservative party prefers to put responsibility before recess, then we will stand the consequences.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I remind my hon. friend from Edmonton that the time for the recess has just about gone. May I also remind him that one day a week or so ago the Prime Minister, in response to questions we asked him, did agree that if we got this debate over during the time a recess was still supposed to come, he would bring on the pension legislation and let it go through the first stages so it could go to a committee before any recess. I submit that the argument that we are merely depriving ourselves of a recess no longer holds water; the recess time has gone and we all know there is not going to be any recess. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, since we are here to do the business of the country, I think it is up to us to discipline ourselves so that we pay some attention to the business that really deserves our attention.
I want to say some things about this debate to the two main groups in this House of Commons. I am going to address myself first to the Progressive Conservative party and then I am going to address myself to the government.
What about the Speaker?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) has made a very important objection.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, I think it might result in better progress in the house if we were to listen to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) without continued interruption.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman is obliged to address himself to the Speaker and not to the Liberals or the Conservatives.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I quite enjoyed the interruption made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere, who is technically correct. I was speaking in a rhetorical sense. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make certain suggestions to the members of the official opposition and then to the government and to its supporters. I trust the hon. member for Lotbiniere will agree with my putting it that way.
That was his first lucid remark.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker- and I hope my Conservative friends will take this seriously, even if they do not like its coming from me-I believe they owe us in the house and they owe the country an honest, straightforward statement as to what their purposes and their intentions are in this debate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, "honest" has an unfortunate imputation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) does not like my use of the word "honest", so I will take it out. I ask for a straightforward statement by the Conservatives of their intentions and purposes in this debate. Maybe there is some other intention than the two that occur to me, but it seems to me it is one or the other.
What are yours?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I am trying to get parliament back on the rails.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
One intention of the Conservative party in carrying on the debate at length

and the statistics I gave can hardly be denied-may be to discuss the matter thoroughly and fully, to bring up all the angles, to go into the matter from every possible aspect. That is a legitimate purpose. But if that is the purpose of the Conservatives, let them say so. If that is their purpose, they should be willing to agree to extended hours of sitting so there can be time for that full debate they feel to be necessary.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
If that is their purpose, Mr. Speaker, I call upon them to say so and to take a position consistent with that purpose. On the other hand, if their purpose is to prolong the debate so as to prevent a decision being taken, I think they should say so, not only to us out in the halls-where they do say it to us-but here on the floor of the house.

If it is their intention to keep this debate going through all of September and into October; if it is their intention to keep it going until we get to the next interim supply time and thus force the government either to suspend the flag debate or to ditch it, I think they should say so.
If they have a purpose other than these two, then that is for them to say. But for us to go on from day to day and for parliament and the country not to know what this chamber is being used for is not fair to parliament, is not fair to the country and is not fair to the great history of this nation. I call upon them to tell us which of these purposes they are pursuing.
The ensign is part of that history.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Is their purpose full and free debate? If so, we will co-operate in providing the extra hours to make this possible. But if it is to prevent a decision, let them say so, in order that the house may know where it is and what it has to cope with.
Now through you, Mr. Speaker, I want to say something to the government. If it is declared to be the purpose of the official opposition to have full and free debate, and if that is straightforwardly their position, I think the government should co-operate by providing the extra hours so that we can take a full decision. The government should make the declaration, in addition, that there will be no closure or any attempt to foreclose this debate.
We have already seen through that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: There is nothing to be seen through. I am speaking frankly and openly, and it is plain to be seen if hon. members will look at it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We are on extended hours now.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) says we have extended hours now, and that is right. But if the purpose is simply to have a free debate in order for us at some point to get to other matters, I suggest that we should be willing to extend the hours still further. We in this party are prepared to do that and I hope there might be the necessary consent to make it possible.
If the other reason for continuing this debate is the true purpose-if the aim is to prevent the making of a decision and that is
Canadian Flag
made clear by the Conservatives-then I suggest it is up to the government to face that situation and to try to decide what to do about it.
I have three suggestions to make to the government. I have already made the first one but let me put it in different language.
I suggest that the government should be prepared to sit it out. By that I mean that the government must eschew-I was accused of being a preacher so perhaps I can use that word-any thought of closure in any form. It must sit this debate out.
The second suggestion I make to the government is that it must keep the door open for any kind of conference which will resolve the issue. The last time the Prime Minister made a statement on the meetings of the party leaders he did say something to that effect at the end of his remarks-that the door would still be open. I plead that that door be kept wide open and that at any time when it is possible a conference should be held, either on the debate itself or on the design of a flag. It seems to me that referring the matter to a committee-unless all five men get together and agree on it-is just delaying the issue. If there is any chance of the five leaders getting together on some kind of compromise on the design, I hope that such a conference might be held at any time.
The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smallwood) who spoke earlier this afternoon asked me whether I was having any correspondence with the Legion in Winnipeg with regard to my position on this flag. Yes, I have had correspondence with the Legion officials in Winnipeg. It is the kind of correspondence which goes back and forth between people who, if they have different views, still respect each other. If I had known that that reference was going to be made I would have brought down with me the last letter I had from the Legion. There was one sentence in the last letter which I had from the Legion in Winnipeg which struck me rather forcibly. The writer of the letter, who was one of the officials of the Legion in Winnipeg, said to me- this was when he thought the issue was just about over-"It is too bad there could not have been some kind of compromise". I congratulate the Legion wholeheartedly for that position. I think it is wrong to suggest that the Legion is an uncompromising organization. In the Legion's own language is the comment that it is too bad there has not been a compromise. I urge the government to keep the door open for a conference at any

Canadian Flag
time, either between the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition or among the five party leaders, so as to achieve some kind of compromise which will produce a design. Toward that end, despite what has been said here, I am not concerning myself in these remarks with the design of the flag, because I do not think that is as important as finding a way to resolve the issue and thus save the good name of parliament.
There is one other suggestion I would make to the government, and I make it in as pleading terms as I possibly can. All of this is based on the second premise that the Conservative party will tell us that its purpose is to prevent action being taken. If that is the case then I urge the government not only to sit it out with no thought of closure, keeping the door open for conferences to take place, but also to arrange that from now on the flag debate take place on only three days a week. I should like to point out that I am trying to be reasonable and I am suggesting a practical proposition. I therefore propose that from now on we have one day a week on estimates, as is now the case, three days a week on the flag, and the other day, which I suggest be Monday, on other legislation. There is the Canada pension plan.
It is not ready.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
There is redistribution. There is the railway legislation and there is the Bank Act. There is all kinds of other legislation. My hon. friend says it is not ready, but I urge the government to get it ready. The government did say a week or so ago that if this debate is over before the proposed recess we might have the pension plan. Let us get at that, and also at the national labour code. These matters have been promised since the start of the session and the list is a long one.
I believe that if there is no option but to sit out a long debate on this issue, with the resultant damage which I feel is being done to parliament in the eyes of the people, we could correct that image considerably and improve our position a great deal if each week while this debate continues we spend one day on estimates and one day on these other important items of legislation. Then if hon. members knew that the session was being planned in that way there would be no temptation to protract the debate on other legislation on Mondays or to protract the debate on the estimates on Fridays. In this way we could start to redeem ourselves and

get some business through and make things look a lot better than they do now.
I do not mind the interjections and the points of order which have been raised during the course of my speech; a speech like this is bound to invite the kind of comments I have heard because I have been treading on toes. But I hope I have been treading on toes of members on both sides of the house. I understand the position of a government faced with a protracted debate- and I am not using that awful word that people do not like to hear-which is spelled out by the statistics I have given. Even if the government feels this is wrong and that it is being dealt with unfairly by the opposition, it is still the government. It is still responsible for parliament and it is still responsible to the people of the country for this institution, and it should lean over backwards to take the kind of steps which will make this parliament look much better than it has looked over these past three or four months when discussing this issue. The best way to do that is for everyone to agree to let the debate end and get on with other business. If we cannot do that, then I call on the government to accept the proposal which I have made and to limit the flag debate to three days a week, with one day on other legislation and one day on estimates. If we do this kind of thing and hold conferences among the house leaders regarding business, conferences on redistribution and on the Canada pension plan, and leaders' conferences on the flag, because we are reasonable and grown up people, I believe can do something to save this institution and make this present parliament, not one which will look bad in Canadian history but one which might yet be regarded as one of the better parliaments in the history of this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I would be delighted.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Does the hon. member not see that there is a principle involved in the flag debate, the principle being the preservation of our history and traditions, as exemplified in the Canadian flag which some people are anxious to discard?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I think a much greater principle is involved. I do not find fault with those who feel as they do about certain designs for a flag, but I feel that the institution of parliamentary democracy is far more important, and it is that which we should primarily aim to save.

Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also agree that there is a further principle involved? We have heard a great deal from the official opposition in respect of a free vote. Would the hon. member not agree that hon. members should be allowed a free vote, and that this issue should be allowed to come to a vote?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe I answered that question earlier in my remarks. I think that parliament should, after a reasonable amount of discussion, have the opportunity of making a decision. I also think that some of the rest of us should have an opportunity to put our proposals before this house. Technically speaking, although the debate has wandered all over the place, we have been debating since June 15 a Conservative amendment and a Conservative subamendment. We would like a chance to debate a New Democratic party amendment to the main motion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: At what length?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: For a reasonable length of time. I think one or two days would be sufficient.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit one more question? Does he not realize that the proceedings of this house, as well as the legislation that is brought before it, is the responsibility of the Prime Minister, and that when such legislation bogs down it could be completed almost immediately if the Prime Minister would allow this matter to be referred to a committee?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I accept the point made by the hon. member for Wellington South, that the responsibility for organizing the business of the house and for what happens in the house rests with the government. That is why I made my appeal to the government, that being faced with these difficulties in respect of this subject it ought not require parliament to spend all week on it. I think the committee idea is a possible one, but apparently the five leaders cannot agree on the terms of reference and the various arrangements. That is why I called upon the Prime Minister and the government to keep the door open for conferences of this kind.
If my hon. friend feels I have directed most of my fire against those who have kept this debate going, perhaps he is right; but I have also called upon the government, in spite of
Canadian Flag
the feeling it may have that it is facing difficulties, and facing the kind of position it ought not to have to face, to realize that it is still the government's responsibility to find a way out of this mess. I believe if the government accepted my proposal, that one day a week be used for legislation, one day a week for estimates and three days a week for the flag debate, with the absolute understanding that there would be no closure of any kind, we would get along much better. Perhaps it would not be long under those circumstances before we could reach an agreement on a proper modus operandi.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. gentleman permit me to ask a question?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Yes.

Does the hon. gentleman not think in fairness to the Prime Minister he should have reminded the hon. member for Wellington South that the Prime Minister indicated he and the leaders of the three smaller parties were agreeable to forming a committee; if there was a reasonable time limit on its deliberations?
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
I asked that question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
I am speaking to a question of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Has the right hon. gentleman not already spoken?
I am rising on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I have not already spoken.
I hope these remarks will be counted as his speech.

Mr. Speaker, I advise the hon. gentleman that his summary is entirely incorrect. As far as the suggestion made by the other hon. gentleman, that his plan would be one that could be acceptable, I rise also to say that we will fall in line with that 100 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, before the hon. gentleman replies, and since this discussion is being treated as a question of privilege, and my accuracy has been contested, I point out that when the Prime Minister gave his report, the leaders of the three smaller parties spoke, and the right hon. gentleman

Canadian Flag
.spoke. At the end of that statement the Prime Minister indicated that he had accepted the principle of establishing a committee, if there was a reasonable time limit placed on its deliberation. The right hon. gentleman himself confirmed what the Prime Minister had said.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that Hansard will reveal the situation more clearly. There were two points made. I took the stand with respect to such a committee, that in view of the fact that the Liberal party has its major ally in the Creditistes, who are 100 per cent in support of removing the union jack, and that with two or three exceptions the general view held by the members of each of the other parties was that the union jack should be removed, while this party stands in favour of preservation of that part, of our heritage and the heritage as well of the French, if the majority of that committee was to make a decision, the decision would be made before the committee started, on the basis of the representation on such a committee. If the decision was to be based on an 80 or 90 per cent basis, and that is the only way in which a flag should be imposed on the people, we would gladly accept that suggestion. That is our stand now. However, to say that whatever report the committee brought in and if it was only a majority decision, the debate should be limited, would mean that we are beaten in advance in respect of the stand we are taking.

Mr. Speaker, since my veracity has been questioned I feel I should put on record again the words used by the Prime Minister on August 21, which will be found at page 7113 of Hansard. The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether I am in order, but I did not make any statement except on the facts of what occurred at the meetings. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition-and I am not complaining at all about it-referred to the suggestion that a committee should be established to look into this question. I think I ought to put on record that we on this side are not opposed to such a committee, but we do not think such a committee should meet for an indefinite period of time and thereby unduly delay this matter. In addition, we believe that the report of this committee should be subject to a time limitation of debate when it is received by the house.
In other words it is perfectly clear that the government as well as the leaders of the other three parties-quite a substantial majority of this house-were in favour of having a committee with a time limit, and a time limit on the debate afterwards. The right hon. gentleman uses words seeking to distort what
IMr. Pickersgill.]
was said, but he will not be able to distort the facts.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to engage in an argument with the hon.
gentleman, but when it comes to distortion, he is the past grand master.
I am not even in the same league.

That is right, you are in
the bush league.
Mr. Speaker, the point I am making is this. There were two principles advanced in respect of the establishment of a committee. We believe that a committee could meet and consider this matter. I said three months should be the period beyond which a committee should not meet. The Prime Minister, as I recall, and I am speaking from memory, said that he thought three weeks, or thereabouts, would be sufficient. I said they should have a free vote, and then if the recommendation made by that committee was substantially unanimous there could be no question as to whether we would agree to a limitation on debate in respect of that committee's report. The view of the other leaders generally was that the usual rule should apply and that a majority should be sufficient. If we accept that and allow the 15 members of that committee to decide the issue we might just as well not have a committee at all, because it would consist of seven Liberals and one representative of each of the other parties. If only one of those members, perhaps the Creditiste member whose party is entirely united, were to decide in favour of removing the union jack and having no vestige of the union jack in the flag, then the committee would simply end there and then. When the matter came back to the house under those circumstances, we would not accept this recommendation. However, if it were substantially unanimous, there would certainly be a limitation and we would be glad to accept a limitation on the basis of a decision of a committee like that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I rise simply to refer to the question the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) asked me, and which started this last bit of demonstration. He asked me if I would make certain remarks about the position of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). I thought I had implied that in what I said, and if I did not imply it, then it has now been put on the record.
There is nothing more for me to put on the record with regard to that, but I should like to say that we have had a demonstration

in the last few minutes of what we all know to be a fact, namely that we are at an impasse; horns are locked and we are in a difficult situation. In the name of all that is right in terms of parliamentary procedure, in the name of the people of Canada, I plead that we find a way out of this. Others have made suggestions, and I made some this afternoon which I hope will be taken seriously by the Prime Minister and by others, despite what has been said.
If I might summarize them quickly, I ask the members of the official opposition to state clearly their intentions; then I ask the government to take these intentions into consideration. If it is the second intention, namely to go on at length, then I urge the government to do three things: One, sit it out without any resort to closure of any kind; two, keep the door open for conferences and compromises; three, plan the week's business in the way I suggested, one day on other legislation, three days on the flag and a day on estimates. I believe if we did this we might start to make some progress.
Accepted here and now; it is up to the government.

I listened with amazement, as I am sure many other members did, to the lecture we just received from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). Of all the people who should be lecturing the house about taking up the time of parliament, he should be the last. I should like to draw attention to the fact that in the 1952-53 session he took up one third of Hansard. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that when an hon. member gets up to speak in this fashion he should practise what he preaches. I should like also to draw your attention to the index from February 18 to July 31 in which you will find there are three full pages given to headings under the name of Mr. Stanley Knowles. The hon. member said that when he was referring to members taking a long time he might be stepping on people's toes, but I suggest instead of that he is stumbling over his own toes. In other words, he is asking for a double standard, one for himself and one for the other members of the house.
Now, Mr. Speaker, had I been given the opportunity to conclude my remarks the last time I spoke on this issue it would not have been necessary for me to take part in the debate at this stage. However, since no one on the treasury benches has replied to the questions I put to them concerning the new
Canadian Flag
flag, and since no satisfactory explanation has been given to the country as to why we should be seeking to scrap our present proud flag, I feel these questions should be placed on the record again. I feel this very strongly, particularly since there has been little or no attempt on the part of government members to justify their stand on the flag. They show no great concern for the effect that the proposed political flag is having on our national unity. I should like also to look into the matter of the so-called free vote that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) now says will be taken on any division on the flag issue. I think one of his supporters, the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) expressed it very well when he said a resolution proposed by the Prime Minister and seconded by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) could not be considered other than a government measure, that it would be regarded as such during any vote that would be taken by his colleagues on the government side. The only way in which a free vote could have been achieved would have been for the Prime Minister to ask one of his private members to introduce the resolution. Had this procedure been followed, I am quite sure the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Mathe-son), who is a co-designer of the Prime Minister's pennant, would have welcomed the opportunity. He may have had some reservations because he is reported to have expressed some doubts as to its proper heraldry. I am sorry the hon. member is not in the house this afternoon-he was earlier-but I am equally sure the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) would have been glad to act as seconder. His great contribution to the flag debate has been recorded in Hansard by a series of, "Oh, oh's".
Now, the little matter of heraldry does not seem to bother the designer commissioned by the Prime Minister to design a flag for him. He is reported also in the press as saying that anyone who did not like the blue edges could cut them off. It does not seem to bother the Prime Minister because, in answer to a question he said Canadians could fly any flag they like. Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, it probably would be much more appropriate if the government were to give to each Canadian a new flagpole rather than a new flag.
While the matter of the flag that Canadians may fly is not too important to some people, I find that the majority of the people with whom I have talked or corresponded have a deep regard for our present national

Canadian Flag
flag. This is particularly true of those who suffered the deprivations, illness, the humility and degradation of the prisoner of war camps. During a recent visit to my home constituency I talked to a Hong Kong veteran who had spent a long period in the prisoner of war compound on the island. He said he will never forget, nor will the Canadians with him ever forget, the day when the red ensign was once more raised on the flagpole over the prisoner of war compound. He said they knew on that day that freedom had come to them once again, and that peace and justice again walked hand in hand across the land once more.
I have with me a couple of typical telegrams which I have received from my local Legions. I think a lot of hon. members have received similar telegrams. One of these was sent to myself and the other is a copy of one sent to the Prime Minister. I believe that the Legions, their families and friends are, generally speaking, wholeheartedly in favour of retaining our present flag, and this is what the first telegram says:
The Crystal City Legion have not changed their stand on regards red ensign and expect your full support.
The other telegram sent to the Prime Minister, with a copy to myself, says:
It is the desire of the Canadian Legion branch No. 21 Manitou, Manitoba, that the red ensign be the national flag of Canada.
If a flag is to have any meaning it must symbolize first of all the people's pride in the nation's past achievements. It must symbolize their love of country at the present and their hopes and aspirations for its future. The part now so recklessly being played by the government with regard to our national unity will foster bitterness and division at the time harmony is so urgently required within the nation itself. Harmony is needed, not so much because we have to face any insurmountable problem but because we have lowered our eyes from the horizon of future greatness to quarrel and oppose each other over the picayune issues of the present.
In this regard I would like to read a news item from the Ottawa Citizen, reporting an interview with a visiting member of parliament from Britain, who discussed this very aspect of Canadian life. The article's heading is, "U.K. M.P. says petty issues hurt Canada," and it reads:
Sir Edwin Leather, a Canadian born member of the British house of commons for 15 years, said Wednesday Canada faces a frightening domestic problem.

The Conservative M.P., bom in Hamilton, said the problem is that Canada has no really serious problems and petty issues thus are debated by government officials.
"The most worrisome part of it is the contempt many Canadians are expressing against their government," he said in an interview.
"And with the (French Canadian) separatist movement making itself heard, petty issues could tear the country apart because no one cares enough to do anything about it."
The Prime Minister by introducing the flag issue into the political affairs of the country at this time is contributing to that image of bitterness that the hon. gentleman mentioned, and is only adding fuel to the heat already engendered by other elements not too interested in national unity. His own members are taking little part in the debate, except to heckle as though it is of no consequence. They are accusing the opposition of a filibuster and in this way they hope to convince the Canadian people that we are wasting parliament's time. They also hope by these tactics to win the debate by default. Let me assure them here and now, and I am quite sure they will get this assurance from other members in this party, that they are not going to win anything this way. The Prime Minister has got them into the mess and he had better start looking for ways to get them out.
Now I have something to say in regard to a filibuster. The Winnipeg Tribune in an editorial in its issue of Friday, August 21, had this to say about the filibuster:
Filibuster of Silence.
The word "filibuster" may acquire a new political connotation before the flag issue is resolved. The Prime Minister used the word in the house August 4 to describe the tactics of the opposition, and it has been employed with increasing frequency by those in sympathy with his desperate plight in parliament.
Oxford defines the word as meaning obstructionist. Mr. Pearson apparently intends it to mean "refusal to enter a debate." Hansard confirms this for there is no debate taking place.
Some eloquent and profound speeches have been made by members of the opposition but the government benches remain silent except for occasional hoots.
Nick Mandziuk (P.C.-Marquette) succinctly defined the parliamentary situation on August 12. In reply to an interjection he said:
"A filibuster of silence."
The opposition has offered the government many pertinent observations, has requested answers to perplexing questions, has invited participation in resolving sensitive problems, and has explored national unity, national history, and national purpose.
But the government supporters refuse to discuss any of these subjects. As an historical episode it will make sad reading for the Canadians of tomorrow when they learn how a government attempted to convert parliament into a flag-making factory.
The opposition's speeches at least will serve as a valuable record on what thoughtful politicians

had to say about the state of our country in 1964. There will scarcely be a word of what government supporters thought for all Hansard has to record about them is: "Some MEMBERS-Oh, oh. Some MEMBERS-Filibuster."
A chill stubborn phalanx of inarticulate politicians is rallied around their filibuster flag and that's how history is made.
Yet we are talking about a debate. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) described this as being a debate. Where are the members of his group who have entered this debate? Where are the members of the government who have entered this debate? Where are the members of the other little parties who have entered this debate? Have they no idea of what their constituents want in regard to a flag? Have they no thoughts about what the country needs to resolve our unity between the two great founding nations? They have no ideas at all, Mr. Speaker. At least, if they have they are not expressing them.
As a matter of interest I would like to mention one more thing in regard to the so-called filibuster. The Prime Minister, in the last revised version of items he wanted dealt with before calling a summer recess, listed six items. Five have been dealt with and we are now on the sixth, the flag issue. The official opposition feels it is important enough to forgo the holidays in order that this whole issue will be settled in a democratic manner.
It has even been suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) that the government bring forward other important legislation so that we can deal with that also. Yesterday he suggested that the farm loans legislation be brought forward, but we found in answer to that question that it was not ready, and there is a growing suspicion among opposition members that the government's other legislation is not ready either, and that in order to play for time its members sit there twiddling their thumbs in a filibuster of silence.
The Prime Minister and some of his colleagues seems to feel that the election promise made with regard to the flag supersedes all their other promises made at that time, despite the fact that it was conspicuous by its absence from the Liberal campaign literature, as the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) has pointed out. It certainly does not appear in the literature which was sent me by the Liberal candidate in my riding. I have a copy here. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, it is about 2 feet long by 6 inches wide. There is fine print on both sides and it is full of promises to the Canadian people.
Canadian Flag
In all this fine print there is no mention of a new flag. It is not my intention to put any of these unfulfilled promises on record because I dislike having my speech cluttered up with trash-and no other name can be used to describe what is apparently nothing but Liberal propaganda.
The Liberal candidate in my riding was really kind. He sent me another pamphlet called "Prosperity and the Farmer". These two pamphlets are published by the national Liberal federation. If any member wants to get copies, the address is 251 Cooper street, Ottawa. Just reading this pamphlet would make any farmer full of anticipation. His mouth would water. However the farmers are still waiting for these promises to be fulfilled. Do you know something: There is nothing about a flag here. It did not offer the farmers a new flag.
Wrong part of the country.

Incidentally it might be interesting to recall an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on August 13 under the name of Mr. Bruce West. This is what he had to say:
Have you noticed how well those new banners are holding up on the radio antennas of those brave souls who are leading the way in our trek out of the valley of colonial humiliation? What the Toronto soot and rain are doing to these pennants shouldn't happen to a proposed flag for Lower Slobovia. Even their most ardent supporters must be wondering a bit about these bedraggled banners which were recently rushed on to the market by some patriot with a fast eye for a buck. After only a few weeks in the breeze, they make a sorry comparison with the historic flag which has been flying in this country for the better part of a century. There's just something about a wet maple leaf on a tattle-tale grey background which fails to stir the pulse, and surely the designers of the proposed new flag must recognize this fact.
I see my time is running out and I must curtail what I had intended to say. The article goes on:
However, perhaps I and many other hundreds of thousands or millions of people in this country are wrong, as we have been told so often in rather rude and testy terms. If this is so, I would like to see it proved in a nation-wide referendum.
We are constantly being told that such a vote would cause widespread dissension in this country. What, pray, do we have now? It is hardly unity.
I am sure that many of us who now oppose the scrapping of our present proud flag now be willing to shut up and bow to the will of the majority if a referendum indicated that a new flag were desired by this country.
It might be painful, but not nearly so painful as the prospect of having this flag foisted upon us by a government which really gives its members no other choice but that of voting for the adoption of a new standard.

Canadian Flag
Now I should like to make a reasonable suggestion to the Prime Minister. I should like to suggest to him that he withdraw the flag resolution until such time as a Canadian government gets a clear mandate from the people on this issue either through a plebiscite or at the next general election. He himself has stated that the people would let him know the answer in no uncertain terms. Let the people give their answer first, before we start messing around with our flag. Unless the right hon. gentleman is prepared to do so he is destroying by a pressed vote what is in reality the very basis of our democratic process. We are not just an emerging nation which would expect a jungle leader to tell us just what flag we must have. We have many years of history behind us, and no flag chosen in such a manner could be considered acceptable to a highly developed, proud and civilized people. By pressing the flag issue to a conclusion, the Prime Minister is scuttling his own legislative program and, in the process, weakening the image of parliament. If our national symbols are to be chosen in this manner, without seeking majority opinion or without at least a willingness to compromise, a strain is being put on our national unity at a time when the utmost good will is needed on the part of every Canadian to ensure that we continue to develop as a nation under the pact created between the two great founding races and adhered to ever since confederation.
I have asked the Prime Minister to drop this issue in the interest of national unity until such time as the Canadian people have an opportunity to express their views either through a plebiscite or at the next general election. We all know where the Prime Minister stands on the flag question. He has made his views known, and he is adhering to them; otherwise the issue would have been withdrawn from the political arena long ago. But we have not heard much from the other hon. gentlemen on the front benches opposite. Mr. Charles Lynch says the Prime Minister's position is weakening in this regard. It would be interesting therefore if the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), for example, were to give us the benefit of his views on this matter. Is he to be the only one in Newfoundland who will be flying this new flag?
Would the hon. member like an answer to that question now?
Order.

No, after I have finished.
[Mr. Muir (Lisgar).)
I would be delighted to give my views by voting if I were allowed to do so.
Sit down.
Then there is the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) -
That was a good long speech, Jack.
Your members shouted him down.
Five o'clock.
