speechtext: There is no agreement that Bill No. S-27 should stand.

The house resumed from Thursday, August 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-27, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada-Mr. Brown-Mr. Batten in the chair.

On clause 1-Number of directors.

Mr. Chairman, this special bill referring to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada has attracted my attention because of comments that I made in this house in December of 1962 and again in 1964 with regard to the contract between the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. Before I make any comments on a matter affecting the Bell Telephone Company I would like to point out that there is no conflict of interest on my part. I am one of the 222 subscribers to the Tiny township municipal telephone system, and since it is a municipal telephone system the taxpayers of Tiny are the owners of the telephone system. We have no plans to sell the system to any other competitor, and as far as I know we have not been approached to make such a sale in order that they may affiliate their services with our very satisfactory arrangements in the township of Tiny.
This telephone system up on the shores of Georgian bay has approximately 200 French Canadian subscribers who are permanent residents of Lafontaine and the township of Tiny, and about 25 English speaking Canadians who are cottage owners in the district. I wish to declare my interest in a telephone company at this point so no one will accuse me of a conflict of interest.
I mentioned in 1962 that the president of the Canadian Pacific railroad and the president of the Canadian National railroad had written a joint letter to the minister of transport of the day, Hon. Leon Balcer, after they had lost a contract which they had held jointly for 30 years with the C.B.C. In the course of a letter to Hon. Leon Balcer it was pointed out that for three different ten year periods the C.P.R. and the C.N.R. together had rendered service in the transmission of sound to the 195 radio stations throughout Canada. In 1962 the C.B.C. called for tenders for this service and the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., two of the most efficiently operated organizations in the Dominion of Canada-and I would even go further and say two of the most efficiently operated organizations in the world-put in a normal tender based on their 30 years of experience.
You can well imagine, Mr. Speaker, their surprise when they were advised some time later that the contract had gone to a competitive system which was able to quote a price 25 per cent lower. It does seem to me that if there is an organization that can operate a business profitably at 25 per cent lower rates than the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. railroads, after
Private Bills
their 30 years of experience in this particular field, we should turn the operations of the C.N.R. railroad over to that organization and probably they could cut the expenses of the C.N.R. by 25 per cent. However, the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. did not look at it in this manner. They wrote a letter to Hon. Leon Balcer pointing out that it was fair to the communications industry in Canada to have a competitor in the field who was able to put in a very low tender for this service and secure very high rates in other fields by representations to other boards or commissions throughout the dominion. The letter, signed jointly by Mr. Emerson on behalf of Mr. Crump, president of C.P.R., and by Mr. Donald Gordon, concluded by stating:
Public long distance telephone rates in Canada are 50 per cent or more above comparable rates in the United States which are regulated by the federal communications commission.
I was appointed a member of the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines this session and we had before us this original application for examination. Some very interesting news came out of the discussions we had.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member but I wonder if he would indicate, for the benefit of the Chair, how the remarks he has made up to this time and which obviously he intends to make are related to clause 1 of the bill now before the committee. Sir, is clause 1 the title of the bill?

speechtext: No. The committee is discussing clause 1.
I thought we were on the title of the bill.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, if the Chair will look at Bill No. S-27, you will see it is an act respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. However, it is not only an act respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada but is an amendment to a previous act which established by incorporation the Bell Telephone Company in the year 1880 by Bill No. C-67. I suggest that the hon. member is in order in making these remarks on clause 1. This bill is an amendment of a previous act that has been, as the chairman will note, amended on at least a dozen occasions over a period of

years. This bill is an amendment to the Bell Telephone act. The hon. member is speaking to the general matter of the Bell Telephone Company and is therefore speaking, in effect, to the act that is being amended by this particular bill. I suggest the hon. member is in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member. As he knows, I am sure, an amending bill does not, automatically, necessarily reopen the discussion on the original act that is being amended by the new bill. The hon. member on this occasion and, if I remember correctly, on a previous occasion suggested that because there is a reference in the marginal note to previous legislation, all that previous legislation is being re-opened by the bill that we have before us. Certainly there is nothing in the standing orders of the House of Commons that says that when we are discussing in committee a specific clause of a specific bill, the discussion can include the principle or the details of the act which is being amended. There are, of course, precedents to support the position adopted by the Chair. We had a very general discussion of this matter when we were on second reading before we reached the committee stage. But certainly at this stage we should limit our discussion to what is before the committee. That is the requirement of our standing orders.

I had read this Senate Bill S-27 several times, Mr. Chairman, and I was of the opinion, and still am-I did not have it before me when you questioned me-that there was only one clause in the bill. Clause 1 says, you will notice:
1. Section 8 of chapter 67 of the statutes of 1880 is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
Colon. Then there are these words:
8. The business of the company...
And so on. I take it, therefore, there is only one clause in this whole bill. Am I incorrect, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Of course not; there is only one clause, but the clause deals with the increase in the maximum number of directors from 15 to 20. That is what this committee is asked to approve. As I said, on second reading there was very general discussion about the operations of the Bell Telephone Company. It was the feeling of the Chair at the time that we should allow a general discussion, but at this stage my suggestion to all hon. members is that the discussion should be limited to the specific matter before the committee.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I remember that during the discussion of this bill before the house the hon. member for Timiskaming asked in rather forthright terms: What is the need for increasing the number of directors from 15 to 20? I hope to be able to show that they need to increase the number of directors from 15 to 20 in order to be able to divide the profits faster. It takes them a little longer with only 15 men dividing them than it would with 20 working at it. That is the reason I rise to make a few comments on this matter.
I was pointing out when I was interrupted, that the public long distance telephone rates in Canada are 50 per cent or more above comparable rates in the United States. That is the flat statement of the president of the C.P.R. and the president of the C.N.R. Before the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee of this house I made some inquiries of Marcel Vincent, president, P. C. Venne, Q.C., vice president and R. C. Scrivener, vice president, with regard to the operation of their organization. One of the things in which I was interested was a statement which was made under examination by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Regan) concerning the increased rates for local telephone service. We were told in the evidence given before the committee by the speakers on behalf of the Bell Telephone Company that when the number of telephones in a local service increases, the rate goes up. This was a rather surprising statement because many of us have had the idea that the rate is usually reduced for bulk purchases-that volume reduces the rate. Evidently the Bell Telephone Company does not work in that way, because as we were questioning their representatives it came out that the rate was raised locally as the number of telephones increased. Then I asked the question, reported at page 429 of the report:
The more telephones there are, the higher the
rate?
Then the vice president of the Bell Telephone, Mr. Scrivener, gave this answer:
The higher the cost of providing the service and the greater value of the service.
That would show that as the number of telephones goes up the cost of the service also goes up.
A little further on in the proceedings I quoted this statement of Mr. Crump and Mr. Gordon to the representatives of the Bell Telephone Company, and I asked them whether they did not go before the board of

transport commissioners and argue that because of the relatively limited number of telephones in Canada they had to have higher rates for long distance calls. Then this answer was given by the president of the Bell Telephone as reported at page 430 of the report:
Whether the percentage is correct or not, the fact is that the rates are higher in Canada than they are in the United States. The development is not comparable at all; we have a very scattered population from one ocean to another.
The Bell operates in Quebec and Ontario; but they refer to the scattered population from one ocean to another, even though the population they serve is more or less concentrated in Ontario and Quebec.
When questioned as to why the rates were 50 per cent higher Mr. Scrivener replied:
Because of the development in Canada, sure.
You thus have it that the local rates are raised because of the increased number of telephones; the long distance rates are high because of the very small number of telephones. If you ever saw a monopoly operating to perfection, Mr. Chairman, I would say that this is the perfect example.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am afraid I must interrupt the hon. member again. I have been listening to him in the hope that he would relate his remarks to the clause before the committee at the moment, but I must remind him of standing order 59(2) which says:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
What the hon. member is doing now is referring to the operations of this company, which to my mind is quite far removed from the subject matter we are required to discuss, namely the increase from 15 to 20 in the number of directors in the Bell Telephone Company. I would ask the hon. member to relate his remarks to the specific point.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that the hon. member is talking about something concerned with the expenditure of the taxpayers' money, which is always our concern in this house. Whether the company concerned be Bell or Saskatchewan Telephones does not matter; we are talking about spending the Canadian taxpayers' money and I think this is relevant.

Perhaps I might develop my remarks and show the committee how busy the directors of the Bell Telephone Company are with all their multifarious activities, including the operation of Northern Electric
Private Bills
Company. Perhaps it will then become apparent to the committee how vital it is that there be an increase in the number of directors in order to look after the multitude of duties they have imposed upon themselves- in the opinions of many, quite unnecessarily.
I thought when I mentioned that the rates are increased locally because the number of telephones increases, and that the long distance rates are increased because the number of telephones is limited that you would be interested in a statement accompanying the shareholders quarterly review of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, summer 1964 issue, in which the subscribers are given comparative rates to show how the rates have dropped for three minute daytime station to station calls from Montreal to Vancouver. In 1949 it cost $7 for a three minute daytime station to station call Montreal to Vancouver, and in 1964 it costs $3. This is a tremendous reduction, from $7 to $3, in a matter of 25 years. I am not too sure whether this is because of the tremendous increase in the number of telephones in Montreal and Vancouver-because we are told that it is because of the increased number of telephones that the rates go up-or whether it is because of a decrease in the number of telephones. The Bell has already told us that where telephones are scattered the cost must be high to cover the costs. They have explained some of the reduction in cost by pointing out that technological advances are benefiting all long distance telephone users, but when a caller requires personal service to ensure locating a particular person he waives some of the advantages of automatic operation and faces the effects of rising labour costs. Improved long distance service and rate reductions have been accompanied by rapidly growing use of the company's long distance facilities. Microwave systems can transmit large quantities of information over great distances and difficult terrain more economically than is possible with wire and cable systems. These are technological advances well known to the public of Canada, and they believe that they should be taken into consideration in setting both local and long distance rates.
In connection with this application for an increase in the directorate I would draw your attention to part of the annual report of the Canadian National Railways for 1963. The hon. member for Three Rivers knew when the contract was given by the C.B.C., after 30 years in the hands of the C.N.R. and the C.P.R., that between them these

people would lose approximately $1 million a year in services. Mr. Donald Gordon, reporting for the C.N.R. in 1963 on telecommunications, stated that net income from all telecommunications services was $5.4 million in 1963, which was down $200,000 from 1962. Mr. Gordon points out that the C.N. telecommunications net income was down $200,000 from 1962. The C.B.C. contract, which the C.N.R. had lost was worth $500,000 a year to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must again interrupt the hon. member and ask him to co-operate with the Chair. The Chair has brought his attention to standing order 59(2), which I will read again:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
Certainly the hon. member will admit that what he has been saying during the last few minutes is entirely irrelevant, as far as the Chair is concerned, to the clause before the committee. There are rules of procedure which must be respected by all hon. members and I ask the hon. member's co-operation in referring as expeditiously as possible to the clause of the bill now under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I find the remarks of the hon. member most timely. I believe that those remarks have something to do with these operations and with the particular clause that is before us. In fact, I am eagerly awaiting his further remarks in this regard so that we may then know something about this before it is dealt with by the house.

Mr. Chairman, I point out that the bill now before us, respecting the Bell Telephone Company, provides directly for the addition of five members to the board of directors, an increase to 20. I think you, Mr. Chairman, should give some consideration as to why this board should be increased from 15 to 20 members. I suggest any increase in a board of directors is contemplated for one of several reasons. Surely a board of directors has a purpose and a relationship to the operations of the company. This company is asking for an increase of five in the number of directors. I think it is reasonable to our discussion to ascertain why the number should be increased by five, and the function to be performed by those additional members. I think we should be made aware of any situation that has developed in this

country which would warrant such an increase.
It is my information that when a company requires an increase in its board of directors it is because of an expansion in the operations of the company or because the company is amalgamating with another company. Such a required increase might also be necessitated by a proposed increase in the capitalization or expansion of the company. I feel that members of parliament have a right and obligation to ask why a board of directors should be increased.
We have no indication as to who the additional five members might be. We do not have any information about their associations with other companies. I suggest the hon. member is not in a position to tell us who the members are or why they are being appointed. I think it is your responsibility, Mr. Chairman, to allow this discussion to be broad enough so that we may obtain answers to these questions. What purpose will these additional directors serve? What is wrong with the company at the present time, necessitating an increase in its board of directors? I suggest it is your responsibility, Mr. Chairman, to allow hon. members to find out, through the hon. member for York-Humber, whether or not the increase of five members to the board of directors of this company will be in the interests both of the company and the people of this country. I suggest, therefore, that the hon. member be asked to indicate why the officials of the Bell Telephone Company feel an increase in the number of directors on the board is necessary.

Mr. Chairman, I think the gentleman who has just spoken should direct his question to the Minister of Transport. The hon. member will recall that not long ago he voted some $86 million to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways. Let us go back to where this whole thing started.
The Minister of Transport is not here.
He is not usually here, but that makes little difference.

Mr. Chairman, I thank you for your comments, and those members who have participated in this matter, in an attempt to show the relevancy of my remarks in respect of whether there should be five more directors added to the board of the Bell Telephone Company.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that when the railways, canals and telegraph lines committee met I raised a question about the C.B.C. contract. I asked this question directly of the Bell Telephone representative although for some reason or other it was not caught by the official reporters. The question was asked at the end of that committee's meetings. I said, would one of the five new directors be a representative of the C.B.C.? The Bell Telephone Company representatives simply smiled and said, no, they had not given consideration to that idea. I thought
Private Bills
such an appointment might have been a fitting reward for taking a contract from a crown corporation, such as the C.N.R., and giving it to a private organization, so that the crown corporation could show that it was down $200,000 next year in net revenue while at the same time it was down $500,000 in gross revenue. Perhaps that is beside the point.
Perhaps the increase by five in the number of directors of the company was necessitated by the company's great interest in the Northern Electric Company, which is considered by many as a subsidiary of Bell Telephone. During the meetings of the railways committee we made a number of inquiries relating to the connection between Bell Telephone and Northern Electric. The board of transport commissioners had made a report, shortly before the Bell Telephone Company made application for this increase, which indicated that Bell Telephone was entitled to own Northern Electric. In the evidence before the board of transport commissioners, a copy of which I have before me, appears repeatedly the statement that Bell Telephone Company owns 90 per cent of the stock of Northern Electric. By the time the parliamentary committee got around to sitting in respect of this application for an increase in the number of directors, as we were informed by those representatives who appeared, Bell Telephone Company owned 100 per cent of the shares of the Northern Electric Company. That statement is repeated two or three times in the evidence taken before that committee.
Mr. Chairman, several hon. members have commented favourably in respect of this application because there are manufacturing companies and offices of the applicant located in their constituencies. I should like to point out for the benefit of the members of this committee that there must be a riding in this Dominion of Canada in which there are employees of Industrial Wire and Cable Company. In respect of the reference to the board of transport commissioners in connection with Bell Telephone and Northern Electric, hon. members might be interested in knowing that most of the employees of Industrial Wire and Cable Company reside in the riding of York-Humber. I have good reason for participating in this debate, because of the interest of the employees of Industrial Wire and Cable. That company has an industrial factory located at the intersection of highway 27 and the Queen Elizabeth highway, in the township of Etobicoke part of which is in the riding of York-Humber. The Industrial

Wire and Cable Company acted as an inter-venor in an application-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry I must interrupt the hon. member. I feel his comments at this point are irrelevant but in any event his time has expired. I have taken into account the fact that there were several points of order. He has been given an additional seven minutes time to compensate for the time used in dealing with those points of order.

Mr. Chairman, when this matter came on before I had a chance to make a few remarks but I did not get an opportunity to make some remarks I intended to make. I do not wish to repeat myself, but I tried to point out then that I had read carefully the evidence before the committee of this house and was unable to find any sound reason for the request for the expansion of the number of directors. The answer was that they needed more leeway, they needed the vice presidents to get acquainted with the board of directors.
However, I want to deal with a broader aspect of the matter today. As the members of this committee are well aware the Bell Telephone Company is a privately owned monopoly in charge of a tremendously important service. Now, that fact is no reason for the refusal of any reasonable request when the company comes before this house. On the other hand, the fact that they come and ask for an increase in the number of directors enables parliament, and I think imposes upon parliament, an obligation to inquire as to necessity for the increase and to ask some other questions concerning the company's public responsibility.
It is well known to the members of this house that this is a private monopoly, but it is a monopoly with great public responsibility and public interest. This is partly served by making its rates structure subject to control and investigation by the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. I am quite sure that the members of this house and the members of the committee do not want to usurp the functions of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. However, we have the right to inquire whether that degree of investigation is dealing adequately with the public responsibility of the Bell Telephone Company. I have a copy of the proceedings before the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada. It is only, I think, about 600 or 700 pages, so I do not propose, in the time available, to bring all these matters before this committee.
[Mr. Cowan.1
This transcript concerns an application of Industrial Wire and Cable and deals with the matter raised by the hon. member for York-Humber, namely whether it was legal for the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, under its limited charter, to own shares of Northern Electric Company, a manufacturing company. Now, this question was dealt with by the board of transport commissioners and they held the Bell company legally entitled to hold these shares. What I think has not been called to the attention of the committee is that there was a further application made to the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada and, so far as I know, this has never been dealt with. Certainly, the committee has never been told whether or not it was dealt with.
As I say, there was an additional phase to that application and that was to find out whether the board of transport commissioners, by reason of the fact that the Bell Telephone Company owned all the shares of Northern Electric, was entitled to review the financial affairs of Northern Electric. This question was adjourned until the question of the legality of the ownership of the shares of Northern by Bell Telephone could be determined. This first question was determined, namely the responsibility of Northern Electric to account to the board of transport commissioners; but so far as I know, and I have the records here but perhaps the sponsor of the bill could tell us some time, the second question never seems to have been looked into.
We have a situation wherein the Bell Telephone Company comes before this house seeking an expansion in the number of the board of directors. We are not in a position to know whether or not, by reason of this link between Northern Electric, the manufacturing company, and Bell Telephone, this large aspect of the work of manufacturing is under any review by anybody, including the board of transport commissioners. I am not the first member of the committee to raise this question. It was raised by the hon. member for Broadview quite early in this debate, on July 18. He said he was not just concerned with whether or not this ownership was legal, but that he was concerned about the question of whether or not this publicly owned monopoly which is under the jurisdiction of the house and which is so important to Canada was, by reason of its ownership of Northern Electric shares, really under the control of this committee and of this parliament or whether a device, as it

were, had been discovered whereby a substantial portion of its operations was not under any control at all. The hon. member for Broadview raised the question, but no answer was given.
It does seem to me that if this house is asked to increase the number of directors, with no reason given but the company's desire to have more leeway, then this house has a right to inquire whether or not, in fact, the application before the board of transport commissioners has ever been dealt with. The question remains open. I submit that before this bill is dealt with, that sort of question as to the responsibility of this company which affects the rights of so many people, should be answered.
Another question that I feel could be answered is the following: In many countries throughout the world they have not adopted either a complete system of private ownership [DOT]or complete public ownership of a public monopoly. In Scandinavia they have adopted a system whereby there is partial ownership by a minority, and there are minority appointments to the board of directors. You have therefore a privately owned company with vast connections, but with representatives of the public on that board. I believe if the sponsor of this bill could assure us that some of the five directors would not be just people with business connections but rather that they would be people with responsibilities to the people of Canada, thus assuring to the public a greater degree of responsibility so that hon. members would have the right and opportunity to find out whether the rate structure was being adjusted in some way [DOT]or other by arrangement with Northern Electric or other companies, he would find we were pleased to give our approval to the bill very quickly.
We have been told that the additional appointments may be vice presidents who are already serving the corporation. I would urge the sponsors of this bill, therefore, that they should seek to answer some of the questions I have asked and some of the questions aked earlier in the debate by the hon. member for Broadview. They should seek to assure this *committee that this would be the result of the request. As I have said, I have read all the evidence in the committee and I could not find anything but the most vague statements that the company wanted more leeway. I believe the parliament of Canada is entitled to be treated with a little more respect by an organization with this wide, major public responsibility.
Private Bills
So far as I am concerned, I do not wish to obstruct the company's receiving any reasonable request that will add to its efficiency or to its responsibility to the public for the tremendously important service they give. However, until these questions are answered, and answered to the satisfaction of hon. members, I feel we should not pass this particular bill. Let them tell us why they need five directors. Let them tell us if the additional directors will add to the public responsibility of the board. Let them tell us whether Northern Electric, which is a wholly owned subsidiary, is to be subject to public regulation by the board of transport commissioners. If they answer these questions they might receive better co-operation from members of this committee, including myself.

Mr. Chairman, during the past few private members' hours I believe there have been attempts to talk out this bill, No. S-27. Members of the New Democratic party have suggested the appointment of five government directors, and there has been some suggestion of nationalizing the Bell Telephone Company.
In my opinion the Bell Telephone Company is one of the most efficient and well run companies in the country, and is better run privately than it would be as an arm of the government. It may be that at one time or another most subscribers to the company have felt they have not been fairly treated by persons answering their complaints. Generally speaking, however, the company is acutely aware of its public image and is sensitive to the quite frequent charge that it is a monopolistic giant and that it is callously indifferent to complaints from its subscribers.
I have a suggestion which might satisfy the objections of members of this committee and which would at the same time be of advantage to the company. I believe that eventually an ombudsman type of individual should be appointed within the Bell telephone organization, and possibly appointed on the recommendation of the federal government. Such an ombudsman individual would shift much of the burden of criticism which the company itself bears now, and such an appointment would meet the objective of the New Democratic party in their suggestion for the appointment of five directors by the federal government.
I have no desire to delay debate on this bill. I simply feel that if the company and this committee gave consideration to the appoint-

Private Bills
ment of an ombudsman within the Bell organization it would be a way out of the impasse that we seem to have reached on this bill.

As the hon. member for Greenwood has said, Mr. Chairman, we do not want to delay unduly the passage of this bill, but the questions we are raising are serious ones and we want to have answers to them from the sponsor of the bill. We are all impressed by the Bell company, the importance of the good work it does and the good public relations it enjoys throughout the country. We are not the slightest bit interested in holding the measure back, but the hon. member for Greenwood has raised a very serious point that I believe it is incumbent on the committee to discuss, and I do not see how we can do that until we have some information from the sponsor of the bill.
It is obvious that the bill is not going to pass this evening, and I hope between now and next week the sponsor of the bill will get in touch with whoever had him sponsor it, will raise with them the points we have raised, and that he will come back next week, or whenever we reach the bill again, and make a statement with regard to the matters we have raised.
To refresh his memory, our main objection is that this is a private corporation managing a very large section of the public business, and we are not convinced that it is proper for such a corporation wholly to own a subsidiary when that subsidiary's financial statements are not available for public scrutiny. It is widely suspected in the electric business in Canada that Northern Electric has a two-price list, one for the Bell company and one for everybody else, and there is a wide suspicion a lot of profits are being hidden in this wholly owned subsidiary.
Before passage of the bill we would like an undertaking from the Bell company and Northern Electric that their financial statements will be made available for scrutiny and examination by members of this committee. We do not think this is unreasonable. After all, the Bell Telephone Company has been granted a very important monopoly by this chamber and it has a very serious duty to the public in general, as indeed to the members of this committee. Therefore because of the fact that this wholly owned subsidiary's financial statements are not available we want to see them and satisfy ourselves that there is nothing wrong with the financial relationship between Northern Elec" trie and the Bell company.
[Mr. Watson (Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie) .1
The hon. member for Greenwood also indicated our view that we think it is a reasonable proposition that members of the public should have representation on the board of directors. Indeed, we intend to move an amendment that three of the directors be appointed on recommendation of the lieutenant governor in council. I think the public ought to have representation, rather than bank directors and presidents of other corporations. I would like to see educational institutions represented on the board of directors. In short we want to see-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Which lieutenant governor in council?

I am sorry, I meant the Governor General. We feel it would be in order for appointments to be made on the recommendation of the Governor General, and we hope the sponsor of the bill will go back, put these two propositions before his principals and let us know what their answers are. I want to emphasize as strongly as I can that we are not interested in holding up the bill just for the sake of holding it up, but we are thoroughly convinced both these propositions are sound and that they raise very serious questions with regard to the matter. We will not let the bill pass until we do get serious consideration of these two very important proposals.

Mr. Chairman, I too should like to make my contribution to this debate on the bill now before us and which provides for the appointment of five additional members to the board of directors of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
I wonder whether such an increase in the number of directors would make for a more efficient administration of the affairs of this company.
Apparently, according to several members I have already heard, the manner in which the company is run leaves something to be desired.
For my part, if I were convinced that the addition of five directors would change in some way the administration as it is now, I would be willing to let the bill pass as quickly as possible.
On the other hand, I wonder whether this would improve the situation.
At any rate, in our districts, we take exception to the manner in which this company is administered and to the service it provides.

For instance, in the Beaupre district of my riding of Charlevoix businessmen and business concerns in small towns located ten, 12 or 15 miles from Quebec city have to pay long distance rates for their calls to Quebec city. This adds up to huge amounts and hinders the development of our area.
To prove my point let me read a resolution passed by the various councils of our municipalities. Here is the resolution introduced at the regular council meeting of the municipality of St. Fereol:
Whereas the residential and commercial development of the Beaupre coast is contingent upon free telephone communication between the municipalities concerned, on the one hand, and Quebec city on the other, it is moved and seconded... that the municipal council of St. Fereol support whatever action the telephone division of the Beaupre coast regional development committee sees fit to take, such as the sending of a petition to the Department of Transport in Ottawa."
That resolution was moved and passed by the municipal councils of Chateau Richer, St. Ann parish, St. Ann village, Beaupre- The Chairman: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I must remind him, as I did for members of the committee who spoke before him, that comments made at the committee stage must be strictly relevant to the clause under consideration.
I would therefore, ask the hon. member for Charlevoix to refer to standing order 59 (2) of the House of Commons which stipulates that speeches in committee of the whole must be relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
The clause under study at this time is clause 1 of Bill No. S-27, providing for an increase from 15 to 20 in the number of directors of The Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
I therefore invite the hon. member to limit his remarks to that very thing.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a few words on Bill No. S-27 concerning the Bell Telephone Company of Canada which wants to increase the number of its directors.
I must say that we are not, in principle, against the increase in the number of directors of this company. It is a private company and it is generally admitted that it has rendered great service to society. We want to respect as much as possible the principle of free enterprise; we want free enterprise to remain in Canada.
If free enterprise, as our friends were saying a moment ago, is too ambitious, if it goes too far, if it denies the rights of the community, the government must step in.
As long as this company does not go beyond its rights, that it is not prejudicial to the community, it must be protected, because free enterprise, or private enterprise, is still the best. Nobody can prove that state enterprises are better than private enterprises.
We are then in favour of private enterprise. But if, once again, this private enterprise is too ambitious it rests upon the government to intervene and see to it that it does not hinder the progress of the community in general.
If the rates of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada are too high, it is again up to the authorities concerned to intervene. If this company makes large profits, the government in turn, levies taxes. Speaking of taxes, I believe the purpose of taxes is to cut down the profits of any private company.
We are glad to share in such a project. We wish, in every respect, to maintain private enterprise in Canada. We are not against

Canadian Flag
any private enterprise or any monopoly so long as monopolies do not deny the rights under which they have secured privileges.
So, Mr. Chairman, I am saying again that ;I wish the Bell Telephone Company of Canada would understand the situation. I know we are doing this company a favour by examining its problems.
It was said, a while ago, that this company was a subsidiary of the Northern Electric Company, a subsidiary of the American company, and so on.
Although this company is a subsidiary of the American company, it nevertheless operates in Canada and all the income derived from this business goes back to its shareholders, and if the latter make large profits, they are in turn taxed all the more under the Income Tax Act.
In any event, I still think that, in spite of all, it is fair to protect this private enterprise.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman? [Text]
Progress reported.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED UNDER ADJOURNMENT MOTION
speechtext:
It is my duty, pursuant to provisional standing order 39A, to inform the house that the question to be raised at 10.30 o'clock this evening is the following:

The hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. La-prise): Labour conditions and winter works- inquiry as to whether the federal government has paid its share.

At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

The house resumed consideration of the motion by Mr. Pearson:
That the government be authorized to take such steps as may be necessary to establish officially as the flag of Canada a flag embodying the emblem proclaimed by His Majesty King George V on November 21, 1921-three maple leaves conjoined on one stem-in the colours red and white
tMr. Latulippe.l
then designated for Canada, the red leaves occupying a field of white between vertical sections of blue on the edges of the flag.
And the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. More.

Mr. Speaker, in this House of Commons I think I am better known as a listener than as a speaker, but I make no apologies whatsoever for rising to make a contribution on this flag question. Indeed, I had a very nice speech prepared, but after the lecture we received from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon I think that even before I make my introduction I should make some observations upon the contribution of that hon. member. It was not unusual for him to adopt the attitude of preaching to the House of Commons about the sins of other parties and other members. He said that we were wasting time, that we were lowering the standards of parliament, and so on. But indeed, Mr. Speaker, if we look at the index of Hansard I have no doubt that this hon. member occupies as much space in the index as I for one occupy in Hansard as a whole. I believe that neither the Liberal party nor the New Democratic party are in any position to lecture to the Conservative party about wasting time in the house. The Liberal party in the 1962-63 session proved themselves to be a more obstructionist party than perhaps we have ever witnessed in this house. Even at the time when the New Democratic party, or the old C.C.F. party, was just a minor group of eight members I think they took more than their share of space in Hansard. Certainly the party to my far left, the Creditistes, and the New Democratic party still, when we consider their numbers, take up much more time in this house and space in Hansard than any of the other parties.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me it is idle for a person to preach to us when he has only to look back on the sins of his own party in this house. I think especially of what has already been mentioned, the divorce blockade-not by a major party but by a minor group in this country, and particularly two members who saw fit to hold up divorce bills in this house, not for 15 or 16 days, but indeed I think it could be measured in terms of months and sessions, and perhaps even years, inflicting personal hardship upon the people who were affected and who had a right to come to this House of Commons to ask for relief.

I believe the hon. member really destroyed his own case, too, when he suggested that we should stop talking so we could vote on the subamendment and the amendment in order that his party could introduce their amendment; in other words, so we could start talking on their amendment. To me that did not sound as though he was wanting an end to the debate in order that we could get on with other legislation. It was not a very convincing case that the hon. member put forward, to my mind.
Typical Knowles tactics.

Then he talked about extending the hours of sitting of the House of Commons. Indeed, this has already been done, and already in the country we are receiving criticism because the attendance in the house is not as it should be when we sit through the noon hour on Fridays. When it comes to his argument that we should get on with other legislation, surely the hon. member realizes it was only at the insistence of the opposition parties that the government was finally forced to bring in their legislative program. We asked for and passed the legislative program which the government wished passed before a recess. If we are occupying the time of the house at a time when we could be on the beaches and in our cottages, there must be a principle behind what we are doing, because certainly we do not do this just because we want to talk.
Stanley wouldn't understand the principle.

The hon. member talked about the number of speeches that have been made in this house by the Conservative members, and so forth. Surely, Mr. Speaker, on a matter of principle such as the flag everyone in this house should feel obliged to speak. He should feel obliged to speak because of the fact that he represents people who I am sure would like to know how he is representing them in this house, and because he has a conscience of his own. Also may I remind the hon. member that there are still a large number of members of this party who have not contributed to this debate at all. These are some of the factors I wanted to raise regarding the speech of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there was nothing in his speech suggesting the setting up of a committee of the House of Commons to which this question could be referred, which would clear the decks for action in this house on other legislation. In fact, we agree with many 20220-465
Canadian Flag
of his constructive suggestions, such as the idea that one day in the week should be left for legislation. I believe the house leader of our party has made suggestions, perhaps not identical but similar in their purport, and I know the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has said he was prepared to accept here and now the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre so far as the bringing in of legislation is concerned. Now it is up to the government to agree to that suggestion and to start bringing in that legislation for which we have continually asked. But where is it? Perhaps it would not be such a bad idea if the Prime Minister of this country sat in on this debate now and then in order to appreciate some of the feelings which are being generated and some of the suggestions being put forward by hon. members of this house, because certainly they could result in a solution of this problem.
The member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz).

I do not want to spend my whole time discussing the speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Speaker. I have listened to many of the speeches made in the house in this debate and I must say that in my opinion they have been far above par. I believe this debate as a whole, considering its length, has been of a quality which we have not seen in this house for many years. Certainly the members of this party could roll out a lot more in the way of emotion and argument than they have. I believe they have been very moderate; I think they have put forward good suggestions; their speeches have been very sincere. I am pleased to note, also, that many of the members of this house who very seldom speak have been prompted to speak in the debate because of the way they feel on this question. I must say that those members have made a distinct contribution by the manner in which they spoke and they are a credit to their constituents.
I am sorry to see there have not been more members on the government side who have spoken. Some of them have been very facetious in their interjections. I would feel from their interjections that they think they have more brains in their seats when sitting than when on their feet. I can assure them that their interjections do not measure up to their expectations.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I do not say this for myself but I trust the

Canadian Flag
hon. member can indicate to the house what change in the design his discourse will bring about.

I am very happy the hon. member is listening so attentively to my speech; if he will contain himself I will get around to that question very shortly.
At the beginning of this debate we had a very broad participation on the part of the members of the Liberal party. Although they were saying that we were filibustering they were almost making speech for speech with us. Then apparently the Prime Minister lowered the guillotine and there was a wall of silence on that side of the house. This was brought to the attention of the public and we are now treated to the spectacle of one speaker per day, so that we cannot say that they are completely gagged. Although some members opposite are very facetious others are very attentive. I have watched their faces during some of the speeches which have been made on this side of the house. I think they have convictions of their own and I wish they would talk about them. I am wondering why they do not. Are they afraid to express their opinions or do they not have any convictions? Are they so divided on that side of the house and so lack conviction that they have nothing to say? I wonder whether they feel that they are representing the opinion of their constituents by their silence. Not all of them are silent. There is the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) who has courage indeed. He made one of the greatest indictments of a prime minister which I have heard in this house. Among other things he said that the caucus was not consulted about the flag, that it was a decision brought in from the top.

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Godin) spent most of his time yesterday afternoon interjecting during the speech of myself and other members in this house. He is doing precisely the same tonight. I would ask you to restrain him or ask him to make a contribution in this flag debate, please.
Go and lick some stickers.
I am sure the hon. member knows as do all hon. members, that an hon. member who has the floor is entitled to speak without interruption. I hope that is kept in mind.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I do not mind these interruptions because they reflect only upon those who make them.
You know where they come from.

I have already dealt with the contention that we are delaying legislation. We are asking the government to bring forward legislation so that it can be dealt with expeditiously, as was the legislation which has already been passed.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is one of the few frontbenchers on the government side to participate in this debate. As reported at page 6956 of Hansard he said:
No one with respect tor our parliamentary institutions would wish to contribute to the filibuster now under way.
The word "parliament" itself derives from the verb "to speak". I am most surprised that the minister, who perhaps was used to exercising bureaucratic power before he became a minister, is now trying to gag his own members and withdraw them from this debate. If they did speak they could make contributions, and I think speech by speech we would inch toward some sort of conclusion which would be acceptable to this parliament as a whole and to the people of Canada.
I must mention the speech of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) because he made some very constructive suggestions. In our amendment to the motion we have asked for a referendum. Then in our subamendment we have made some specific proposals regarding the questions which could be asked relating to a design in such a referendum.
In this connection I should like to refer to a radio broadcast quoted many times here which the present Prime Minister made on December 29, 1961. He was asked: "How would you poll the people on this?"-that is, the flag question. The then leader of the opposition replied: "We would poll the people when we have a general election, and if they don't like the idea of a distinctive Canadian flag which cannot be mistaken for that of any other country they will let us know in no uncertain terms". I agree with this point of view which the leader of the Liberal party expressed at that time.
I also think the people of Canada agree with it because there have been a large number of letters and representations to the government asking for a referendum. I refer to the Ottawa Citizen of June 4 where in an article by Norman Campbell headed "10,000 send views to P.M." one of the categories the letters fell into was those calling for a

referendum on the flag question. So certainly the view of the then leader of the opposition was supported by the people.
Then in the Ottawa Journal for June 16 there is the headline over a Canadian Press dispatch: "350 ft. ensign petition to P.M.". I might just quote shortly from this article, which says:
A petition bearing 17,873 names, mainly from Toronto and southern Ontario communities, was left at Prime Minister Pearson's office Monday urging a national plebiscite on the flag question.
I might point out, Mr. Speaker, that the geographical areas referred to are mostly represented by members on the other side of the house.
I am not an Orangeman but I have an article here from the Saskatchewan Leader-Post of June 18 which is headed: "Orangemen ask Pearson for flag referendum". I also have an editorial from the Telegram of August 22 under the caption "Ask the people". It goes on to say:
The voice of the people can be heard on this issue only through a national plebiscite...
Here is a matter which touches the hearts, the emotions, the loyalties of virtually all Canadians. A parliamentary vote that would destroy the country's flag would leave deep and festering scars for years to come.
So there is certainly the feeling among the people of the country that they want to have a voice in the selection of the flag which will fly over them.
Perhaps the reason they want to have a voice is the manner in which this flag resolution has been brought before the House of Commons. I want to return for a moment to the radio interview which I mentioned given by the then leader of the opposition on December 29, 1961. He was asked: "But you do think the country needs this symbol to hold us together?" and he replied: "Yes; I think it would be a good idea to have a distinctive Canadian flag in the interests of national unity". I emphasize the words "in the interests of national unity". We just have to look at what has happened in this country since the Liberal party took office to see that if there is anything which is needed in this country it is national unity. Unfortunately, everything which this government does tends to divide this country further and further. In another answer the Prime Minister went on to say: "We should try to solve these problems in a manner which will create the minimum of division and the maximum of unity". That is a good way of putting it, and I agree. I think that if we are going to bring in a new national flag it has to be done with a minimum of division in this country, and 20220-465J
Canadian Flag
certainly the Prime Minister of today is not living up to his words of yesterday.
When the Prime Minister was asked: "What about Quebec; would they want the fleur-de-lis on it," Mr. Pearson said: "Well, we would have the Quebec members of our cabinet decide what the design would be". Perhaps it was the Quebec members of the government that designed this flag.

Mr. Speaker, will the hon. member permit me to ask him whether he is aware of the fact that the Prime Minister categorically denied ever having made that statement? I am sure he would not want to repeat something that was misreported and categorically denied by the Prime Minister.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. Is it necessary that hon. members of this house must listen to the Minister of Transport, who is completely ignorant of the facts?

Mr. Speaker, I do not mind the interjection made by the Minister of Transport. I think probably I am one of the more placid members of this house. I was not aware of the fact that the Prime Minister had denied this statement. I believe this report was taken from a tape recording, but if the Prime Minister did not make that statement, I will withdraw the remark, or at least indicate that I am sorry I ever mentioned it.
I thank the hon. member.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: This was a tape recording.
Good night Jack.

Later in this interview the leader of the Liberal party was asked: "What is your conception of the new Canadian flag?" Mr. Pearson said, regarding the design: "Well, I am not going to tell you what the design should be." Mr. Pearson then went on to say: "The government will make up its mind. If I am going to be the head of the government I am not going to tell you what the design is." That does not make very much sense.
I would like to quote from an article which appeared in the Toronto Star, May 20, under the headline "P.M. Told Newsmen of Flag Decision". I suppose he must have changed his mind. Perhaps it would be more clear if I quote a few short lines from this article, because I think this has a bearing on the question. This quotation relates to that meeting of the Prime Minister and newsmen who were called to his home for the unfurling of

Canadian Flag
what was referred to as "his choice", the three maple leaves design. He said-
-he was prepared to have the government stand or fall on the maple leaf flag.
The Prime Minister was careful, however, to make clear that the flag on the mantle was his personal choice.
When we now refer to the three maple leaves design as the Pearson pennant, or something of that nature, I certainly do not think he would now say it was not his personal choice. I am wondering whether it would not have been much more democratic for perhaps a caucus to make that choice, or a committee of this house.
Not only is the motion before the house in the name of the Prime Minister sponsoring a flag design of his own choice, but the Prime Minister said to this House of Commons that if we do not accept this flag then we are going to have an election. I have never heard anything more close to political blackmail than that statement.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to a headline which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on June 18. The headline states: "Regards Both Flag Votes as Confidence Tests: P.M.". Perhaps I might also refer to an article that appeared in the Toronto Telegram of July 20, written by Ronald Collister headed: "Accept My Flag or Else . . . Warns a Defiant Pearson". The article then states:
Mr. Pearson is laying down the law, with fire and fury, after the breakdown of all-party talks on a firm agenda for the next month.
In the Montreal Gazette of August 24 there appeared another article under the heading: "Free Flag Vote, Pearson Calls Off the Whips".
Mr. Speaker, perhaps there is a reason for this turn of events. I have before me an article written by Patrick Nicholson, which appeared in the Quebec Chronicle-Telegram on August 12, 1964. The heading is: "Election on Flag Could Kill Libs".
Perhaps all these headlines are really related one to the other. I think there must be a compromise in respect of this question. Although some might call these compromises retreats, I think the compromises are good. Perhaps one can properly come to the conclusion that if the compromises are necessary they are good. The Prime Minister did not give too much consideration to the whole situation in the beginning, or he would not have had to change his mind so many times. The fact that he is still openminded and willing to change his opinion I think represents good news for this parliament. I think more changes will have to be made.

Mr. Speaker, I should now like to refer to the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) calling for a referendum. I think I have produced evidence showing that there is support among the people of Canada for this position. What might the result of such a referendum be? In my personal opinion I do not think a plebiscite should be held immediately. I agree with the original view of the leader of the Liberal party, that the time to call a referendum is at the next election. If the next election is held a year or two from now I think that would be an appropriate time to hold a referendum, because by then all the emotion that has now been created may well have subsided and we would be able to obtain a more accurate reflection of the views of the public than could be obtained today. I recall one politician who on many occasions said, when the sea is whipped up into fury and the waves are riding high, surveyors do not measure the height or depth of the land, but wait until the sea is calm. Perhaps that thought has some application to this present situation.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer now to the results of some polls which have been held. A Canadian Press dispatch in Winnipeg of June 29 appeared in the Ottawa Citizen and states:
A flag poll at the eight-day Red River exhibition here saw 41 per cent of 15,000 persons indicate a preference for the red ensign as Canada's national flag.
That poll was not conducted by the Conservative party, but was sponsored by the Manitoba New Democratic party. It showed 32 per cent of those polled in favour of a tri-maple leaf flag, 15 per cent in favour of a new flag with one maple leaf, and 12 per cent in favour of a new flag with some other design. Seventy four per cent of those polled favoured a national referendum on the flag. Certainly if one requires a sampling of public opinion, that is it, and it indicates that we should hold a referendum on this subject.
Mr. Speaker, in the Evening Telegram of June 10 appeared an article under the heading: "Flag Straw Vote Ends... Ensign 773; New Flag 332". I believe that poll was held in Newfoundland and should be of special interest to the Minister of Transport.
In the Montreal Star of July 21 appeared an article under the heading: "Red Ensign Advocated by 149,465". Perhaps I should read

a short part of this article, which states as follows:
The office of the state secretary has received 149,465 signatures on letters and petitions since July, 1945, favouring retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag, the Commons was informed yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, I think that article gives some idea of what the people of Canada are thinking, and would indicate why a referendum should be held on this flag issue. I do not think the Liberal party should be afraid of a referendum or plebiscite. The red ensign is leading in nine provinces.
On a national basis, as has been pointed out, the figures are, red ensign, 27.9 per cent, maple leaf flag, 39.6 and others, 15.4. Certainly, they have nothing to fear if they feel the people of Canada really want this three maple leaf flag. This is the way to get it, to have a referendum.
In this party we have generally supported the red ensign. I am not speaking here solely as a supporter of the red ensign. I think I can be a little broader in outlook, Mr. Speaker. Last December I conducted a survey in my own riding, and this was before all the emotions had been stirred up. The survey was quite a wide one but there were some flag questions included. At that time, 10 to 1, the people of my riding were in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag. The margin was something like 52 per cent to 48 per cent in favour of the red ensign. However, since that time, since the time the three maple leaf flag was unfurled, there has been a considerable change on the part of those who wanted a distinctive flag other than the red ensign. Many of them have now decided to support the red ensign because they feel it is a far superior design to the one proposed by the Prime Minister. I agree with them because, personally, I do not like the three maple leaves. I would prefer one maple leaf.
I believe we, in this party, are being very broadminded. I do not believe we have been such diehards, because not only are we suggesting a referendum but our subamendment provides a wide scope for the questions to be placed on the referendum. We have given four choices to the people of Canada. The first is the red ensign. The second is a modification of the red ensign. The third is the three maple leaf flag, and the fourth is a single maple leaf flag. Since this proposal has been made in the subamendment there have been a number of speeches made in this house in which the suggestion has been made this question should be referred to a committee. I am wholeheartedly behind this idea.
Canadian Flag
I believe that this party would be prepared to accept a reasonable deliberation by such a committee. If the government insists on a time limit so far as the committee is concerned, certainly that would be no stumbling block.
I feel that one of the things the committee could consider would be a design that might have almost unanimous approval. If such unanimity were reached and such a flag were brought back to the house, I believe it could be adopted without too much debate and there would be no need for further reference to the people. If the small group of members comprising this committee were unable to agree, then perhaps they could clarify the questions that should be asked on this referendum. Of course the red ensign question is very clear. The question of modifications on the red ensign could be considered by this committee and perhaps they could suggest a modified red ensign that could be placed on the referendum. Then we have the three maple leaf flag. It could be considered as it is or perhaps suggestions may be made to modify it, such as those made by A. Y. Jackson. Perhaps his design could be considered, and a final recommendation brought forward. Then we come to the one maple leaf design. Of course, there are hundreds of one maple leaf designs. Perhaps if this committee could not agree on a design they could at least narrow down the number of one maple leaf designs. All these designs could be put on the ballot.
Then I believe the committee should report to the house and this question should be put to a referendum. This issue should be taken out of the House of Commons and referred to the people as a whole. If even a small group cannot decide amongst themselves, then we in this larger House of Commons have little hope of reaching agreement on a design. I feel that if this committee chose these four designs and then the people declared themselves on those designs, the design chosen by the people would automatically become the flag. I think the suggestions made from this side of the house are worthy of consideration. I believe the very fact that we are willing to give the people this scope, and are willing to accept the decision which the people may make, whatever it may De, certainly shows that we are not so stubborn or so rigid in connection with one design that if the people of Canada as a whole voiced their opinion, we would not be willing to accept it.

Canadian Flag
Surely that is the spirit of compromise. I do not believe we have to apologize for it. I think that is the spirit in which we must consider this question. I see my time is running out, Mr. Speaker. Incidentally, the Winnipeg Free Press, which is certainly one of the greatest supporters of the Liberal party, says in its editorial of August 21:
Thus a national flag is being bom in the worst possible circumstances-in political bitterness, party strife and parliamentary manoeuvring. The outcome could easily be a flag that would be looked on by many not as a symbol of national unity but as a political flag of divisiveness and controversy.
Farther down, the editorial reads:
Why could not Mr. Pearson-in the hope of securing some harmony within parliament-ask to refer the flag motion to a parliamentary committee composed of representatives of all parties?
Then, it goes on:
-it would give parliament a voice in choosing a national flag...
And farther down it says:
-would make a start towards restoring public respect for parliament.
What we are asking, Mr. Speaker, is being asked in the spirit of compromise which has been accepted by the leader of the Liberal party and the Prime Minister, by shifting his position from time to time. I do not consider it is dishonourable to do that. I think he must shift his position once more if he is really interested in the unity of this country. I am not so old and so bound to tradition that I am unable to sense that I must exhibit a spirit of understanding and compromise, if this nation is to emerge united and strong after this debate. I am not so young that I do not feel a sense of loyalty or devotion to the symbols which have signified and represented something of the richness and uniqueness of my country. I recall the credo of the Progressive Conservative party which is contained in the phrase, "The vision to create, the courage to retain." I think if anyone searches within himself for a guideline to direct his thinking to contribute more to the interest of Canada and all Canadians, then that is a very worthy one to remember. I think if we directed our thoughts along the lines of that phrase, we could contribute more to the interest of Canada and of Canadians than if we were to apply any other philosophy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must say that it is difficult, if not impossible, to achieve a unifying symbol in a country that is itself not unified. This was stated in one editorial. Perhaps it was the thought of the Prime Minister that at this time when the very threads of confederation seem to be bursting, that the

various opposing elements in this country could unify behind a symbol of Canada such as a flag. This may be a legitimate desire on the part of the Prime Minister in introducing this resolution. However, just as the bicultural commission, instead of unifying the country has already tended to crystallize the English and French apart from one another, and at the same time has sent a wave of nationalism through the other ethnic groups which was not evident before, so the introduction of the flag resolution has tended to divide this country along Anglo-Saxon and French lines.
Because of this, like many speakers before me I deplore this debate taking place. I deplore that the Prime Minister has not seen fit to postpone the flag debate until there is more evidence of unity in the country and when the rallying around a flag would be more natural. The introduction of a flag should be at a time when jealousy and distrust and hatred are at their lowest ebb. That is not the case today.
Because I am neither of Anglo-Saxon nor of French origin, I deplore more than most the fruitless, the useless and the damaging forces that have been set forth in this flag debate. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) has already expressed not the joy but the sadness of those of us who are considered the third element in Canada to see the two factions at loggerheads with one another, especially when these two factions, whether accurately or inaccurately, are considered the founding races in Canada.
Also, in making a contribution to this debate I would like to say that too many Anglo-Saxons and too many French people forget that they are not the only ones in Canada. Today, just as in this House of Commons, every group is a minority, with the Anglo-Saxons, the French, and the other groups combined forming almost equal factions. The fact that Canada is a country of minorities has often made me feel proud because I could see so much unity in the diversity about us, until lately. I grew up in the west where people settled in colonies of Ukrainians, Germans, Polish and French, and it may be interesting to note that in my own riding I have more Indians than I have people of French origin, although we do have a few communities of French people-and I may say they are very fine people.
I might digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to read a letter from one of our original citizens, the Indians. This letter is significant because it comes from one of the seven Indian chiefs I have in my riding, a man who

was a past chief of the Indian Brotherhood of Canada, and in his letter he says:
I have just returned from a meeting in Winnipeg. We were shown the proposed new flag. None of the chiefs like it. They wanted to know where the union jack was. It is the flag of our Queen and should be part of the flag of Canada. All of the chiefs in Manitoba wanted the red ensign to be the official flag of Canada. Please speak for us on this point.
I am enclosing a petition of the people on my reserve.
In the Toronto Telegram of June 13 there was a letter to the editor from a Peter Jackson, headed "Indian Treaties in Jeopardy." It read as follows:
Apart from other aspects of the flag situation in Canada, as an Indian I am deeply concerned about the apparent determination of the government to impose a new national flag on the Canadian people.
I am fully conscious of the significance of the union jack in some form to the majority of Indians in Canada. Most of the treaties which Indians signed included a reference to the "flag", then the full union jack, and the final approval of these treaties involved the presentation of a flag to the Indian tribes concerned as an earnest of good faith.
The present proposal of a flag bearing only a few maple leaves is very disturbing as it appears to place in jeopardy the treaties signed in the past for "as long as the grass grows, the sun shines and the flag flows in the breeze."
Certainly no Indians, nor Eskimos, have been consulted about a Canadian flag, and, for Indians at least, it has a greater significance than to any other people in the dominion.
Perhaps this again is a reason why we should have a referendum.

Mr. Speaker, as for the point of order, I wish to say that all those interruptions have taken about three or four minutes of my time and I would ask you to allow me a few minutes longer after my time is up.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out to the hon. members opposite that I do not intend to show as much moderation in my remarks as my colleague who has just resumed his seat, for he does not have to put up with this flow of propaganda organized by the Liberal machine-

*-so that this flag issue may become simply and purely a partisan issue.

I am coming to it and I can assure you that you will be surprised.
Let us hear it.
Mr. Speaker, throughout all the years I have been in this house, I never had to read my speech, but in view of present circumstances and of possible misinterpretations-
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I would ask you to call the hon. members to order. I take this opportunity to tell them that when the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), who is assistant whip of the Liberal party, read his speech, we did not interrupt him in any way at any time.
Because he made an intelligent speech.

We let him read his speech to the end. I would therefore ask you to call the hon. members to order. They should be as polite with the members of the opposition as were the latter with the government supporters.

I wish to point out to the many visitors listening in the galleries that the members of the Liberal party and the minor parties behave like school children during this debate on the flag issue. They show partisanship in their interjections, because instead of rising and stating their point of view, they have incessantly interrupted and insulted me, but I do not worry because they are too low to reach me. I think that they show the depth of their genius and their broad-mindness.
Mr. Speaker, the debate on a national distinctive flag exceeds in my opinion the scope of ordinary legislation coming under administrative responsibilities. It is a question which affects those who are not affected by a piece of legislation and I am thinking of those who, on account of their age, are out of the reach of existing laws. The choice of a distinctive national flag has this characteristic; it concerns every citizen of Canada for centuries to come.
What we should deplore most is the turn taken by the debate because of the blunder made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in steeping the flag issue in political partisanship. The introduction of the resolution as an ultimatum including the adoption of two flags in the statutes of Canada as well as two national anthems-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

-is, at once, unacceptable to any member worthy of this name.
Mr. Speaker, there is no point of order; it is all part of dilatory measures of obstruction.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It is prohibited to read a speech and, what is more, a speech written by someone else. It is obvious that this speech was written by Mr. Allard.

This is a kind of stupidity which shows the hon. member's personality. Not only does he annoy his own government, but he annoys all hon. members of the house and the people who elected him; they will get rid of him, I am convinced, at the next election, because he has shown no seriousness in any of his interventions.
