Mr. Speaker, I should like to go on to say that if we are now facing a difficult situation in this house, it is because the man who received the Nobel peace award, since it was said that he had showed great qualities as a mediator on the international scene-
Hear, hear.

I am glad to hear this applause, because that man, as I was saying, proved to be unable to settle, in his own country, a situation as delicate as the flag issue and he introduced in this house a solution that produced confusion.
If I accuse the Prime Minister of such misconduct, it is because he was very keen on introducing under his own name a proposal which should have been kept outside party lines.
However, he is not the only one responsible. Pressed by the panicky mob of his supporters who saw their political ambitions fade away at the thought of a general election, he abandoned principle for partisan strategy.
Mr. Speaker, our country has never experienced so much uneasiness as it has since this Liberal administration took office.
Retreats, reversals, abdication of principles have shaken the confidence of the people in

the authority of the government, and separatism exploded under this irresponsible administration.
Why, Mr. Speaker? Because French Canadians felt they were let down by co-operative federalism and by the retreats of the Prime Minister.
How can the Canadian people have confidence-

-in a man who, on May 19, 1964, said about the flag:
I have pointed out, and I think I should make it quite clear, that when the government submits to parliament a matter of policy-

-parliament must-

Mr. Speaker, I was just going to say that the Prime Minister, when he introduced his resolution on June 19, stated that a principle was involved and that the government would stand or fall on the decision of the house.
And now that man, going back on that principle, told us a few days ago: The vote on the flag issue will not be considered by the government as a vote of confidence.
As stated by Mr. Claude Ryan in that same editorial of Le Devoir of August 22 last:
We wonder if a man is serious when he says, one day, that there is a principle involved in a certain question and, the next, changes his views.
Further on, Mr. Ryan states:
We sincerely believe that there is nothing more serious than the public reversal by the head of a state on a question of principle.
Not only has the Prime Minister contradicted himself on a question of principle, but he has lied openly. This charge is not made by myself but by two of his colleagues, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Francis) and the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), who said as much during their participation in the debate, when they stated that the Prime Minister had not told the truth when he claimed that he had consulted the Liberal caucus on the choice of the three maple leaves.

Mr. Speaker, why did the Prime Minister not think of including in his flag a symbol showing that our country is Christian?
Oh, oh.

I see that some people shrink at the thought of including a Christian symbol on the flag, but that does not surprise me on the part of some hon. members opposite.
Mr. Speaker, would the reason be found in the news item published in the great Montreal paper La Presse in 1955, on the second page-
Who wrote that speech?

Toronto, 1955. Press release of the Canadian Press.
The Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Canadian secretary of state for external affairs, stated yesterday evening that he doubted that organized Christian religion would be able to unite the peoples of the world.
And he listed the weak points which prevent Christendom from accomplishing such a task.
Past experience makes us question the importance of the part played by organized Christian religion in recognizing that interdependence of nations, which will lead to greater unification in the world.
And the release adds, that, according to Mr. Pearson:
The truth is that after 2,000 years, Christianity remains the religion of a comparatively small minority. Though missionary zeal is often praiseworthy, adds Mr. Pearson, it often results in contempt for other people's beliefs.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the reasons which perhaps caused the Prime Minister to omit in his distinctive Canadian flag design all Christian symbols which might honour this country among Christian nations.

Mr. Speaker, here is my question of privilege. While the hon. member for St. Mary talked about Christianity and the need for more Christianity in Canada giving us quotations of 2,000 years ago, he called the hon. member for Lotbiniere a fool. I say this. Although for the last 2,000 years the same Bible has been preached in Canada and elsewhere, there are still people like the hon. member for St. Mary who incur damnation every day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would ask the co-operation of all hon. members not to raise alleged questions of privilege or points of order to interrupt the hon. member who has the floor and who is entitled to be heard without interruption.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all members on this side of the house. My question of privilege arises out of the remarks of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) when he referred to reading speeches in this house. I want to point out that the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. McLean) the other afternoon never took his nose out of his notes, and that is a far cry from what the hon. member who now has the floor is doing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. For the third, fourth or fifth consecutive time, there is obviously no question of privilege whatsoever and I fail to see how hon. members' privileges are affected by the point raised at this time. I again ask the co-operation of all hon. members to allow the hon. member for St. Mary to continue his remarks uninterrupted.

Mr. Speaker, I now rise on a question of personal privilege myself. I would like to submit to Your Honour that I have been continually interrupted while making my speech.
I have been insulted, although I do not care from which corner these insults come. I think these people are causing more disruption and obstruction by their interventions in these proceedings than we ever did in the house. I think the time they have taken by these interferences should be given to me to compensate for the injustices now being caused to me.

Mr. Speaker, I am very sorry for having said-First of all, I did not use the words imputed to me by the hon. member for Lotbiniere to the effect that I said that the Prime

Minister had lied. I said that it had been said by his own colleagues.
I am sorry for having said that the hon. member for Lotbiniere is a fool and is completely lacking in intelligence; I am sorry for having said that the hon. member for Ville-neauve is lacking judgment. I never spoke so many truths in so short a time. I hope that the house will put up with me.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the Prime Minister because of the procedure he followed in introducing this resolution in the house, sowed distrust. He shook up forever the confidence of the people for the function he represents or which he should represent.
The man who once said:
That he preferred to live under the communist yoke rather than be killed by the atomic bomb-
-once again showed an uncommon weakness.
If the Prime Minister was not afraid to face an election, he would not have backed down. Therefore, it is not judgment which motivates his decisions, but fear. And fear is a rather bad adviser.
The Prime Minister was, at first, afraid to lose face. That is why he did not consult the party chiefs. He was afraid of an election, and that is why he sullied the matter of principle. He was afraid of being overthrown by his own members on the second part of his resolution, with regard to the adoption of the union jack as a second flag; that is the reason why he avoided the confidence vote.
The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) has become the official propagator-I mean official propagandist-of the Liberal government-
Not propagator, but propagandist. You do not know how to read.
The hon. member for Lotbiniere does not understand what I am saying-*
The hon. member for St. Mary cannot read.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Lotbiniere is a neurotic, I shall ask him to leave the house or to respect those who have the floor, as well as your authority.
Mr. Speaker, I ask you to prevent the stupid member for Lotbiniere from interrupting me at every turn for nothing.
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Lotbiniere rises to a question of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, we are all fed
up of hearing the hon. member using abusive language and insulting everybody, calling one stupid and the other idiot.
I cannot understand that you should have ruled that such language was parliamentary. The hon. member uses coarse language when he does not read the speech of Mr. Allard. I would ask him to read correctly the speech written by Mr. Maurice Allard; that is all I want. He should abide by the rules, be polite and refrain from using coarse language.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for St. Mary.

Mr. Speaker, now that the show is over, I will proceed with my remarks.
For the past few days, service stations have been able to write to the Prime Minister, attention of the Minister without Portfolio, to obtain at low cost, pennants, flags, beer mugs and shields with the three maple leaves of the Prime Minister.
If supplies run short, the minister may import some at short notice from Japan, because deliveries are made very quickly.
The three-leaf flag has become a profitable business for the traffickers of the country. The government has suddenly become a distributor of souvenirs. It is even surprising that the Minister without Portfolio is not seen with a cart in front of the parliament buildings auctioning the Pearson's proposal to visitors.
We, on this side of the house, want a distinctive Canadian flag-
Now, you are reading much better.

You are now speaking better yourself.
As far as I am concerned, I shall vote for a distinctive flag of which we can be proud, a flag that we shall display with pride, that we shall respect and which will be respected throughout the world; in short, a flag that will make us feel Canadians first and foremost.
But how could we be proud of the Prime Minister's suggestion if it has to be forced upon us by a majority vote when it has been soiled by the partisan ambitions of the Liberals or by amateur hucksters.
If the Prime Minister is really sincere about his distinctive Canadian flag project, he should leave partisanship out of it. He should accept alternatives reflecting the aspirations of the Canadian people in this matter.
Canadian Flag
I have expressed my views several times on this question. Several Conservative members expressed their views on it in the house between 1958 and 1962. Those many suggestions on a Canadian flag were made by Conservative members who were then in power and not afraid of assuming their responsibilities, and they were respected by the leader of their party, the then prime minister and present Leader of the Opposition.
Never did we get, from the Liberal opposition of the day, any suggestion for a distinctive Canadian flag, but we, the Conservatives, got down to work.
We began to find a solution to that problem which had been neglected for 22 years, under the careless Liberal administration of our friends opposite.
Mr. Speaker, we now have to deal with a subamendment-
About time.

In my opinion, it is imperative-and I think my friends' time will not be wasted-to bring to light now the conflicting stands taken by certain hon. members or party leaders, just to show to what extent this debate has managed to distort the objective we should all strive to achieve.
On the question of the referendum, for instance, the Ralliement Creditiste have actually disowned their past and their constituents. The member for Villeneuve, a few moments ago, intervened in the debate and he accused the opposition of trying to filibuster in this debate by proposing a referendum.
Now, on March 5, 1963, during a meeting he held in Montreal, with all his candidates of the island of Montreal, he said that if his party came into office, he would call a referendum on the question of a national flag within six months. And here is the man and his party-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. I wish the hon. member for St. Mary would have the honesty to quote word for word what I said about a distinctive national flag in 1963, because he is mistaken. Someone else said that within six months a plebiscite or referendum would be requested or held to choose a flag. If the hon. member for St. Mary claims that the hon. member for Villeneuve himself requested a plebiscite, he is lying barefacedly before all hon. members of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask you to have the charges laid by the hon. member for Villeneuve withdrawn because, according to Beauchesne's, when an hon. member rises

Canadian Flag
in the house, he is responsible tor what he says and if he must submit evidence to support his remarks, otherwise he can be accused of lying.
Give us proof.

In reply to the hon. member for Villeneuve, I have here an article from the March 5, 1962 issue of La Presse, which reads thus:
Mr. Caouette's promise.
A referendum within six months on the flag issue.
It is written out in full and for the future guidance of the hon. member for Villeneuve, here is what it says:
Six months after coming into power, the Credi-tistes will ask the Canadian people, by way of a referendum, to choose a distinctive national flag.
Such was the statement made on Sunday afternoon by Mr. Beal Caouette, national associate leader of the Social Credit party, who was the chief speaker at a big Social Credit meeting in Montreal.
Should the hon. member wish me to keep on reading, I will give the names of all the candidates attending that meeting.
Name them.
Withdraw.

I think that when the hon. member for Villeneuve accuses me of lying, I wonder who is the liar in view of the evidence. I shall not require an answer, for charity's sake.
Mr. Speaker, on this matter of a referendum the hon. member for Villeneuve is not the only one who has taken a contradictory stand. On January 23, 1961-and I see the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) taking out his references-on January 23, 1961 in the house, the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, seconded the former member for St. Boniface, Mr. Laurier Regnier, who moved a bill to provide for a referendum concerning the adoption of a Canadian distinctive flag. The Minister without Portfolio supported this resolution; but now that he is a member of the cabinet, he rejects the proposal for a referendum. Such a contradictory stand is not in accordance with the soundness and sincerity we should bring into the debate concerning the adoption of a distinctive national flag.
I believe that if our hon. colleagues on the opposite side, as well as the members of the smaller parties, have not got enough courage to rise in this house and express clearly and positively their points of view on the flag

issue, but are satisfied with mere interjecting or charging the official opposition with filibustering, I believe they are dishonest and their present stand is contrary to the dictates of their conscience, for in taking such an attitude, they only prejudice the cause they should support, that is to gain the confidence of the people in their members by discharging their responsibilities and their duty as representatives of the people and the Canadian population.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
The hon. member has been wriggling for 20 minutes-
No, for 45 minutes.
-for 45 minutes-
This is Mr. Allard's speech.
We do not know where he is heading. Could he tell us exactly whether he is in favour of a referendum? In favour of a distinctive national flag?
Order.
What does he favour? We wish we knew.

That is something you
would have to ask Mr. Allard because he is the one who wrote that speech.

If the hon. member cannot see what I am getting at, we know even less what he stands for since, he is now against a referendum whereas he was in favour of it during the election campaign. The same thing goes for the Minister without Portfolio. At the time, he was in favour of a referendum; now he is against it.
By expressing my opinion on this question, I am taking my responsibilities-
Which question?

-and I am exposing the treachery of those who make believe that they are sincerely opposed to the Conservative proposal.
Mr. Speaker, I would ask the hon. member for Villeneuve to remain seated and to stop bothering me. He can speak after I am through and I shall answer-
And I am going to give you a good licking too.
The Creditiste candidate lost his deposit in my riding.
Wait until the next election.

Mr. Speaker, I was speaking precisely on the subamendment, that is on the referendum and my hon. friend is wondering why I do not deal with the matter under consideration. Then if the hon. member is dishonest enough to impute to others the faults he may have made himself, he should have the courage to repeat his statement and assume the responsibility of his assertions. If he does so, I will summon him before the committee on privileges and elections.
As the union nationale.

I know that the hon. member for Lotbiniere is a pain in the neck for the Prime Minister and parliament and I hope he will have medical treatment before too long.
Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister had appreciated that before introducing the flag resolution, it would have been better first to agree on the definition of the term which in my opinion give rise to all his troubles, he would have realized that it was necessary to determine what is meant by the word "distinctive".
For some of my English speaking compatriots, the word "distinctive" has quite a different meaning than for French speaking people.
For them, it can be an alteration of the red ensign, with also a symbol reminding us of the participation of French Canadians on an equal basis. If they are sincere-and I think they are-they are entitled to this opinion. But I feel that while respecting this viewpoint, we must admit that it is neither in harmony with the desire of the majority of the people nor able to establish a real Canadian spirit and to unite all ethnical elements in our country.
For us, French Canadians, this word "distinctive" means something which would not include any sign or symbol of dependence on another country.
We want to be first of all Canadians, proud of our origins, proud of our history. Confident in our future, we ought to accept nothing less than a flag which would be truly ours, which nobody might confuse with another one. Hoisted throughout the world, it will have to be the symbol of a nation on a par with the great powers. And it will open for us the doors to international discussions on an equal basis.
A flag including a foreign emblem would be likely to lower our prestige in the world. It would prove that we are not yet free from
Canadian Flag
our colonial status, while in fact the Statute of Westminster of 1931 freed us from this stigma.
How can we talk of repatriating our constitution if we have not acquired yet the patriotic maturity required?
Do we suffer from a lack of patriotism? Should we not put our country above everything else? If we are able to answer yes readily to all those questions, we cannot accept anything but a truly distinctive national flag without any symbol of subservience.
But if our heart, our feelings, our attachment are not entirely centred on our country, we are not mature enough to ask for a truly Canadian flag and we should talk even less of total Canadianism.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I would like to submit to the house the ten commandments we would be wise to observe if we want to reach a settlement on the flag question. Perhaps I should have submitted them earlier, for our hon. friends opposite would have then controlled their temper.
The commandments would be as follows:
1.	Establish our good faith, explicitly.
2.	Speak on behalf of our constituents, courageously.
3.	Avoid offending remarks, conscientiously.
4.	Eliminate the racial question, obviously.
5.	Avoid claiming that a Canadian distinctive flag is a concession to Quebec, naturally.
6.	Co-operate in finding an acceptable solution, sincerely.
7.	Express our views, freely.
8.	Refrain from distributing the three-leaf flag indiscriminately.
9.	Liberals should express their views, honestly.
10.	Do our duty as we should in this parliament assembly.
And the hon. member should sit down, slowly.

Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, to end this deadlock, the Prime Minister should accept an alternative; he should prove his goodwill to the people by withdrawing his three maple leaves and accepting a compromise meeting the wishes and the aspirations of the Canadian people.
Many hon. members found quite enticing the suggestion made the other night by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent). In fact, many colleagues told me they were quite ready to accept a flag bearing one green maple leaf which would in a way

Canadian Flag
recall the history of our country, a symbol which would not be a symbol of division but one of national unity. The maple leaf identifies Canadian people everywhere in the world, as at the Olympic games for instance. When our athletes go abroad, they wear a maple leaf on their uniforms and this is how they are identified as Canadians.
Hear, hear.

The maple leaf is an accepted symbol, but there has never been three maple leaves on coats of arms, jackets or uniforms of our representatives abroad. And I hope that the Prime Minister, if he wants to show his sincerity in coming to an agreement on that question, will accept this alternative and change his flag so that it will be acceptable everywhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously I do not intend tonight to speak on the merit of the resolution which is before the house. I plead guilty; I was the first to object, for the purposes of the discussion which followed the introduction of the subamendment, to speeches foreign to that measure.
Therefore, tonight I will keep strictly to the question of procedure, that is to the question of deciding which procedure must be admitted in a effort to put an end to the debate which has been going on for so long already.
[Texti
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made certain suggestions about the conduct of the business which, if I am restating them correctly, were as follows: First, the official opposition is to state clearly their intentions in this debate. Then, he asked the government to take those intentions into consideration. He then urged the government to Jo three things: 1. To sit it out without any indication of closure of any kind; 2. To keep the door open for compromise; 3. To plan the week's business from now on with Mondays taken for legislation, Fridays for estimates and the other three days for the flag debate. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) commented on this suggestion in these words: "Accepted here and now; it is up to the government."
In the early part of his speech, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested that if the official opposition wanted a prolonged debate for the purpose of bringing out every aspect of the flag question the hours of
[Mr. Valade.I
sitting should be extended. I am going to respond to this suggestion here and now on behalf of the government. We would, of course, be glad to get on with other legislation. We think the best way of doing that is to get the flag debate over with. But if that is not possible, we are not prepared to have the time available for the flag debate in each week reduced.
However, there is one way in which the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could easily be carried out right away. The government would be prepared, if the house will agree, to sit on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays, in the evening, eight to midnight. In this fashion the number of hours available for the flag debate would not be reduced. The government then would be only too happy to reserve Mondays for other legislation, on the understanding that the flag debate will be concluded by the end of September.
Go away; by the end of September.
Same old nonsense.
Just a different type of closure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am asking all hon. members to give serious thought to these proposals. I shall try to arrange a meeting of the house leaders of the various parties, tomorrow if possible, with a view to seeing whether they could not be put into effect next week. I hope this ready acceptance by the government of suggestions made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be ample evidence that the government is keeping the door open and is ready to consider any reasonable course in relation to the present debate.

Mr. Speaker, as has been quite obvious, it was not my intention to enter this debate at this stage of the proceedings. I think it has been amply demonstrated that my colleagues in the New Democratic party take the same stand. However there comes a time when your concern for your country can no longer allow you to remain quiet. Certainly, the performance of this parliament from the time it opened last February, and more and more in recent months and weeks, leads anyone who has any concern for his country to stop and do some thinking. I think this concern is very well summed up in an article that came to my desk today, and what surprises me is that I think this is the first article this particular writer has ever written with which I could

agree. I am referring to Mr. Lubor J. Zink, and I would like to read his article at this time. He says:
It is safe to assume that, as a result of partisan exploitation of dormant nationalistic sentiments, the flag controversy is by now seen by many Canadians as a symbol of English-French rivalry. In this perversion of the search for a distinct expression of Canada's final stage in her evolution from colony to full independence, most Quebeckers tend to regard the ensign as a reminder of English dominance which they are no longer willing to tolerate. Conversely, English speaking Canadians are led to believe that the maple leaf flag denotes Ottawa's betrayal of all they hold sacred in their heritage. The new flag, they are told by those who call it sneeringly "Pearson pennant," symbolizes Grit abject appeasement of and sellout to the French.
All this sowing of nationalistic mistrust, which cannot but produce a harvest of hatred and strife, is done by allegedly rational men motivated by visions of a strong, united Canada.
One cannot but wonder what goes on the in the minds of these blindly partisan politicians when in the same breath they deplore the fanning of nationalistic ferment in places such as Cyprus. There they say irresponsibly inflamed passions must give way to reason. The world cannot tolerate old enmities to play havoc with peace.
At home, apparently it's different. And when the P.M. at the request of an opposition M.P., calls a meeting of party leaders to see if some acceptable way out of the impasse could be found, the attempt is described by his chief political rival as a sign of weakness.
In this atmosphere no honourable compromise seems possible, unless the electorate shows more sanity than its elected representatives and forces them, through grass root pressure within each political party, to stop acting like a bunch of Makarioses.
I cannot help but wonder, would we have reached the situation we find ourselves in at present if, for example, we had a system like they have in Norway, where the calling of an election is taken out of the hands of the prime minister, where the calling of an election cannot be forced by an obstinate opposition, where they have a party system similiar to ours but where they hold an election every four years, and in the interval they run the business of the country and do not fight the next election every day in the house of commons, as we have seen here for months past.
How did we get in this position? It started out with the stupidity of the way the Prime Minister introduced the flag resolution, where he used his position to present his own choice of a flag and tried to shove it down the throat of the House of Commons when, by admission of one of his own colleagues, it was not even cleared in his own caucus. I cannot think of anything more stupid.
Canadian Flag
I will say that it is to his credit that he has had the common sense to back away from the position he took originally. I wish the same common sense would be shown by others. But just what happened from there? Then the ball was tossed to the Leader of the Opposition, and obsessed with his mad idea that by some design of destiny he is supposed to be prime minister in 1967-Sir John A. in 1867; Sir John D. in 1967-because of this madness he appears to be prepared to destroy this parliament and with it to destroy this country by turning English against French and vice-versa.
I thought you had a little sense.

Unfortunately I thought some of the others had a little sense, but they have proven they have not.
After five months of frustration in this present session we had the rare good fortune of having the Leader of the Opposition ill for two days and away from the house, and in those two days, as everyone knows, we accomplished more than we had in the two previous months. Then a week or two after that we were blessed again. The Prime Minister went to England for a week, and during that week we cleared everything but three items of the order paper.
I think that the best thing we could do, both for the benefit of this house and the country, is if we could send both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition away for two weeks. Then maybe we could get on with the business of the country.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Send them to Hull-spelled H-u-1-1.

Mr. Speaker, I can possibly best sum up with a few words of doggerel:
The Flag Furore of '64.
On parliament hill, we now have a bill
To provide a new flag for our land.
Letters thick, letters thin just keep pouring in
Urging M.P.'s to take up a stand.
With Mike's maple leaves three many do not agree
Some like one, some a dozen or more.
While some would go back to the old union jack,
Some dropping the ensign deplore.
But I hope you'll agree, as you listen to me,
We have more urgent problems than this.
Automation we've found makes the workless abound,
Our economy's still hit and miss.
It would take some vast sums to clear up our slums,
We need medicare, pensions and all.

Canadian Flag
And we surely are fools if we think that our schools.
Can cope with our children this fall.
As on this we reflect I most strongly suspect,
That all this flag fuss and furore;
Has been started I'll bet to make people forget
The grim future we all have in store.
If we don't toe the line, while still there is time,
A red herring, upon a smokescreen,
Is the suitable rag we should wave for a flag,
In a country that just might have been.

Mr. Speaker, now that the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) has raised the level of this debate from a non-partisan level, perhaps it will change the line of approach that I had intended to take during my intervention at this time. Then also we had one of those rare occasions during the course of the flag debate when we had an intervention on the part of a minister of the crown, in the person of the government leader of the house. Unfortunately, as usual, he has completely misinterpreted the mood of the house and he has, as I understood the observations that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) made this afternoon, completely misunderstood the purpose of those observations. The solution propounded by the government leader of the house is a continuation of legislation by exhaustion.
He made a grave mistake last spring by keeping the house continually in session over the Easter period.
Oh, oh.

It was the first time in the years I have been here that members of this house were not permitted to return to their constituencies where they could get in touch with reality and refresh their viewpoint of the problems of the nation.
Would the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question?
Certainly.
Is that what is wrong with the official opposition?

I am quite willing to admit that the fact we have not had an opportunity to renew contact with our constituents has resulted in the sort of mood, the intransigent mood, which prevails at the present time. But if this is a problem with the opposition, how much more must it be a problem for members and supporters of the government who seem to be completely out of touch with public opinion in this nation?

Legislation by exhaustion does not improve the processes of democracy. It is a Pavlovian technique used when the brainwashers want to break down the resistance of those they want to convert to their own opinions. I would have suspected that this suggestion might have come from the minister of propaganda, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) because this seems to be the function he is carrying out as far as his responsibility in the cabinet is concerned.
I had intended to continue this discussion along the lines pursued by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) this afternoon. He was offering to the government a way out of the impasse into which they have led parliament at this time. Certainly, as we have seen during the course of this debate, by the reaction in the country as reflected in the press and other media of information, the government should be looking for a way out. When the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was presenting his academic viewpoints on the paralysis of parliament at the present time he was reminded that it is the responsibility of the government to control the business of the house, and he agreed that such was the case. I asked him a question. I asked him if it was not true that when the executive arm of government, without consulting its own caucus, without consulting its members, decides to bring an issue before parliament which is not only dividing parliament but which is also dividing the nation, that the only recourse which the official opposition has in such circumstances is to bring a sense of reason to the government by means of a continuation of discussion.
There was a conference on peace, order and good government held at Couchiching a couple of weeks ago and Mr. Speaker was good enough to circulate some notes arising from that conference. I intend to quote from page two where some observations are recorded by Dr. Crick, a political scientist from the old country who was invited to speak. The document reads;
Dr. Crick agreed that a system of government should be flexible and reminded the audience that politics is the art of the possible.
I might observe at this point that the government of Canada has placed parliament in an impossible position because it has presented this house with an issue which is bound by the very nature of things to bring about divisions which are always beneath

the surface in a country which can only persist as a nation on the basis of unity in diversity. Later, Dr. Crick emphasized-
-that the functions of the institutions of the government must take account of the changing responsibilities of government, and he felt that the present crisis in British government was due to the fact that the capacity for opposition is weaker than at any period in British history. Parliament, he said, should be a continuous election campaign, a permanent hustings, and it was up to M.P.'s to supply efficient and effective criticism continually.
This is precisely what we are endeavouring to do at the present time. But parliament consists of more than the opposition. It consists also of the backbenchers supporting the government. If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is concerned with the fate of parliament in the present circumstances or during a period of a continued minority, I think he should be equally concerned about the disdain which the supporters of the government are displaying, as far as their responsibilities in this chamber are concerned. They are continuing what the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) referred to as "a filibuster of silence". This has been the subject of comment in a leading article in the Winnipeg Tribune, which I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre must have seen. This silence is expressive of the worst kind of arrogant disdain for their responsibilities to their constituents. Of course I can understand their silence. They are able to say little on this issue because, as the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan), recognizing his own responsibilities as a member of this house, told us. neither he nor any of the government backbenchers had been consulted on this matter. I suppose that if it were not for the rigid discipline which is maintained on the opposite side of the house they would have some observations to make on this subject which would be of interest to this house. But in the circumstances they have nothing to say.
It is more difficult to understand the silence of those who sit on the treasury benches. So far, only one minister has broken that silence, namely the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), except for the intervention tonight of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) which was not by way of throwing light on the reasons parliament had been brought to the present impasse, but rather was to offer more of the same legislation by exhaustion, an offer which will only intensify the unhappy mood which prevails in parliament at the present time.
Canadian Flag
It would seem that even members of the cabinet were not consulted on this matter, because they are not silent on the hustings even though they are silent in this house. Mr. Speaker, I read a voluminous quantity of speeches made by members of the cabinet in various parts of this nation. Indeed so many of these speeches cross my desk that I must confess I do not have time to read them all. I have had come into my hands a most interesting series of speeches made by members of the cabinet on the very subject under discussion in this house-speeches made outside the house, not in this chamber where they should have been made-and I hope to be able to put some of this helpful and useful material on the record before I conclude my observations here tonight. Obviously, with backbenchers remaining silent and members of the cabinet remaining silent, it is easy to understand why there is protest not only in this house but across the nation over the design of a distinctive national flag, to use the classical phrase, that has been presented to this house, and also the method by which it has been presented. These are the main points that have emerged in the discussion up to the present time. This is why members of the opposition are trying to be helpful in providing avenues of escape from the difficulty into which the government has gotten itself. This is not even a party flag. This is not a flag that has come out of the careful consideration of a party caucus, that has been carefully considered by the cabinet. This is a personal flag, a personal design. I do not know who were the advisers to the Prime Minister on that particular design. We know that my very good friend, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) was one of the heraldic authorities who advised on this matter. I would be suspicious of objectivity in this regard, because while the hon. member for Leeds is a very good friend of mine, he indicated during his term in opposition in this house that he was also a very zealous partisan.
Since the flag was introduced into this house there has been a lack of consistency in the government's dealing with the matter. It has vacillated in the most uncertain and confusing manner. It was brought into the house with all the bombast of electioneering flamboyance. It was said that the flag would be flying by July 1 and the challenge was issued to the opposition to move a want of confidence motion in connection with the flag. This is not the way to deal with an explosive subject

Canadian Flag
of this nature. This is inviting difficulty in the House of Commons.
Hear, hear.

Then, Mr. Speaker, the opposition, realizing its responsibilities in such a divisive matter refused to test confidence in the government on the question. The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) accuses the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), as he did just a moment ago, of wanting an election on this issue. If we had wanted an election, we would have accepted the challenge of the Prime Minister when he invited us to move a want of confidence motion on the flag issue during our dealing with supply. The question of an election is not at stake. I could not understand why the hon. member introduced this particular thought tonight, because while it is true that the Prime Minister took fate by the forelock and said the destiny of the government would depend on the decision with regard to the flag, he again vacillated, has backed down, and an election is no longer in question on the issue. What is in question is whether the government is going to continue, to quote the immortal words of the Globe and Mail, "parliament and Canada on a collision course on this vital matter".
As the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) indicated the other evening, the concession of returning to a free vote, taking off the whips in this matter, has come too late because positions have hardened; most hon. members on the government side have declared themselves, some with great searching of souls, as was indicated by the hon. member for Victoria (B.C.) (Mr. Groos) who spoke the other evening as one of the few government representatives in the debate. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this concession is quite meaningless.
The question that arises is, just how are we going to get out of this present difficulty? Perhaps before we proceed to that question we should ask how we got into it. This is the question propounded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) tonight. I think it is a product of the bureaucratic mind. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said that if parliament does not sort itself out we are going to transfer power to the establishment.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: We have done so already.

Well, Mr. Speaker, this has been going on for a number of years in this country. The seat of power is being gradually 
removed from the floor of the House of Commons to the offices of the bureaucrats. This process of erosion is assisted by the silence of the government; by backbenchers who refuse to get up and express themselves on this matter. In these circumstances, this is inevitable. But the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre forgets that there are no less than six members at the highest level of the establishment who occupy cabinet positions at this time. I believe in the Maclean's magazine presentation of the Canadian establishment six of the present cabinet ministers were given the highest accolade; they were called mandarins, and the Prime Minister himself was described as one of the members of the establishment. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask this question. Perhaps the difficulty is that the establishment is too closely identified with the government and this is why they cannot see the wood for the trees. This is why they have precipitated parliament and the country into the present unhappy impasse to which we have been directing our attention.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: If, as he says, the establishment is so closely related to the party in power, does not that make it all the more serious for parliament to follow any course that seems to give more and more power to the establishment?

As the hon. member himself said this afternoon, it is the government that directs the course of parliament. The opposition can only direct its attention to the business that is placed before parliament by the government. As we all know, the opportunity for the opposition to initiate business in this house is restricted to the private members' hour. I think my hon. friend, who has been most active in this area of parliamentary interest, is fully aware of what a frustrating and ineffective aspect of the work of parliament is this particular part of our procedure. So if it is a case of power being transferred to the establishment, we are faced with this unhappy situation-the establishment is closely interlocked with government from the Prime Minister down.
I think we are all aware that the bureaucratic mind is something like the scientific mind. In fact, I think one of the tests of mandarin stratification in the Maclean's article was the necessity of being a Rhodes scholar, and most of the Rhodes scholars

operating in the Canadian establishment majored in social science studies. As I say, Mr. Speaker, the bureaucratic mind is very closely related to the scientific mind, which endeavours to reduce multiplicity to unity. But unfortunately if this process is carried too far in the political realm it leads inevitably to totalitarianism, or at least an overweening power of the executive arm of government. This can make tyrants out of those who merely aspire to clear up the mess. This has been demonstrated over and over again whenever democratic bodies around the world have reached the impasse we have reached at the present time.
Our constitution is dedicated to the fundamental premises of peace, order and good government; and I would remind the house that in order to have peace and order you have to have good government. I do not think we have good government, certainly on this issue which is before the house at the present time. You cannot resolve the problem of national unity in this country merely by making a quick change in symbols. This is political primitivism at its worst. As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), a wise and experienced member of this house, said the other day, it is political ignorance on the part of the government to think that by a sleight-of-hand change in the symbols of this nation they can resolve all the problems of national unity which have been with us ever since confederation. This is to ignore the problems of regionalism, of our vast geography, of the ethnic multiplicity, which was referred to by the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Slogan) tonight, and all the political differences. We have five parties in this house. Indeed, we might say we have seven parties, because there is not unanimity within all the party ranks, as I shall point out in a moment.
On top of this we have endeavoured to apply a political system, a parliamentary system which grew up in a unitary state, to a federal state, but with all its peculiar problems. Some have objected to the idea of a plebiscite or a referendum because they say that this has never been used in the mother of parliaments in Great Britain. But the mother of parliaments is a unitary state. There they have a homogeneous population. They have social homogeneity which we do not have in this country, and whenever in Canada a government has been foolish enough to raise an issue on controversial matters as fundamental as this one before parliament
Canadian Flag
they have inevitably resorted to the referendum technique. Again this was the technique of the Liberals back in the early years of the world war. No leader who understands Canada would proceed as the Prime Minister has on this matter.
We have not only advocated a plebiscite as a way out so that we might get on with the business of the country. As has been pointed out in the debate tonight, the leader of the Creditistes was also in favour of a referendum when he spoke at a rally in Montreal on March 5, 1962, as reported in La Presse. Said the leader of the Creditistes:
Six months after taking power the Creditistes will propose to the Canadian people, by way of a referendum, the choice of a distinctive national flag.
But we have gone beyond that now. We are suggesting a parliamentary committee which, if it was the intention of the government to proceed with this matter, is the way we would normally proceed in the house, instead of making a narrow partisan and political issue out of a controversial subject. The door is still open, and all that is necessary is to have a parliamentary committee representing all parties in the house, as recommended by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), get together and try to come to some consensus so that we might resolve the divisions that are all too obvious in this house and across the nation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the only serious intervention on the part of a cabinet minister pointed out all too clearly that this was an explosive and divisive subject. He referred to filibusters and all the rest of it, but his main thesis went beyond this point. He referred to the division which has arisen in the Progressive Conservative party on this matter. He shed crocodile tears over the subject. But what about the division in the Liberal party which has appeared in this chamber? We have heard members supporting the government most critical of the way this subject has been handled. I am not going to repeat what the hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) has said, but he referred to decision by a rump convention. He also referred to no consultation with members of the party and no announcement in the campaign literature, and so forth.
There is also a division in the Social Credit party. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) the other night did not take a stand either way. He quoted some letters and said, in effect, that some of his friends are for this and that some of his friends are

Canadian Flag
he said: "I am for my friends". That is the classical example of the answer which is given by politicians when they do not want to make a decision on a controversial matter. There is also division in the New Democratic party. The only party which has demonstrated solidarity forever on this matter is the Credi-tistes, which is a party dedicated to extreme viewpoints and issues in this country. I think that speaks for itself.
While the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has not spoken in this debate, he has had things to say on the subject of a distinctive flag over the years. I want to get around now to discussing some of the speeches which have been made outside the house by ministers of the crown. This matter was before Canada in 1954, when the prime minister of that day, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, a responsible leader who knew the political pulse of the nation, refused to proceed with an issue which had been brought forward by a backbench member of the government at that time.
Then again, even before that, I have a report appearing in MacLean's magazine for February 1, 1954, dealing with the debate of that year and it quotes the now Minister of Transport when he was a member of the establishment.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Was he a mandarin?

Yes, he was a mandarin.
The article says:
It didn't come up again until 1944 when another Mackenzie King government proclaimed that the Canadian red ensign should be Canada's battle flag, borne by the troops on D-day and after.
On V.E. day the following year came another occasion when the issue was almost settled. Prime minister King was in San Francisco preparing a broadcast to the Canadian people. He thought he should put in something about the flag.
Jack Pickersgill, then special assistant to the prime minister, asked "Why don't you tell the people this is Canada's national flag, and have done with the argument about it?"
That is in quotations in Maclean's magazine, the article written by Blair Fraser.
No answer.
He is trying to think one up.

Mr. Fraser goes on:
Alas, he was too blunt. People who have read Mackenzie King's diary report that on that day King recorded the incident with the comment that he wasn't going to have such a delicate matter settled by a brash young secretary.
That was 20 years ago. I was only 40.

You're still in the foolish
forties.
Instead he contented himself for the moment with authorizing the use of Canada's battle flag on the peace tower and on other public buildings at home as well as abroad.
Four months later came the order in council which did proclaim the red ensign our distinctive national flag.
That was the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill), a very prominent member of that government. Back in those days he spoke out about what he thought as a Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, the hom
member is something of an historian himself and presumably made an honest living in academic life. I do not think he would want to distort the record. That is not precisely what happened. I made no speech whatsoever about that, but I did have a private conversation with Mr. Mackenzie King in a hotel room in San Fransisco. Mr. Mackenzie King decided it would be a rather good idea to fly the red ensign on the peace tower on V.E. day. I thought that was a good idea too because it seemed to me it was rather more distinctive of Canada than the union jack, which was. flown up to that time.
Mr. Speaker, is the hon. member making a speech, or is he speaking on a point of order?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My understanding is that the hon. minister wanted to ask a question.
I should like the minister to make a speech in this house.
I was trying to liven up the hon. gentleman's speech.

Mr. Speaker, he represents the province of Newfoundland in this house and I am sure the premier of that province would like to hear the minister declare himself heartily in favour of the three maple leaf flag.
Mr. Speaker, I do so. I declare myself heartily in favour of the three maple leaf flag or any flag with the maple leaf as the distinctive Canadian emblem.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the minister hopes to get around this difficulty by making these typical political dissimulations in respect of the two flag concept. Hon. members opposite have criticized us for discussing this matter in a responsible way and say: Let

us vote on the matter. They think a simple vote is going to resolve the difficulty.
Oh, oh.

I would remind hon. gentlemen who are braying from the back benches that the difficulty, the division and the problems of this nation will only begin when parliament makes a decision in such a hypocritical fashion in the hope of getting around these difficulties and divisions by using the two flag concept.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a very serious question. Does the hon. gentleman really believe in the dictatorship of a minority, or does he think the majority has a right to make decisions?
Hear, hear.

They are braying again from the other side. Mr. Speaker, I believe in intelligent and honest discussion of these matters rather than the catcalling that has gone on across the way during the course of this debate. I look right in the eye of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) when I make that remark. He was looking with simulated scepticism as I made that statement, Mr. Speaker.
There have been speeches made in respect of this important issue outside the house by ministers of the crown, and I refer to a seminar that was held at the University of Manitoba last March 7, before the government was even thinking about bringing the flag before parliament as a red herring issue. The Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) took part in that debate. One caption in the Alumni Journal reads:
Mr. Sauvo's "good sense", Mr. Pepin's "charm and wit" set the stage for a day of intensive and interesting discussion of the problem-Canada, one nation or two?
Let me quote what Mr. Sauve said on that occasion in my native province, the province of Manitoba. He said:
Let us not concentrate on what divides us...two nations or ten nations. Let us concentrate on one Canada.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what we are asking this government to do, instead of playing around with the two flags, and all those other things which are designed to divide this nation. If we have two flags we will then have symbolic separation, and that is hypocrisy of the worst kind. We would
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion then have separatism symbolized by the presence of two flags.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on and quote the remarks made by the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve). His solution was not a national flag. His theme involved a national economic policy. He said we must forget about these other extraneous matters and concentrate on an economic policy which will bring about the unity of this country. He referred to the particular economic difficulties of the province of Quebec. He then went on to support enthusiastically one measure or economic policy introduced by the former government designed to deal with this particular difficulty. He then said:
So we have to change, and the only way to change Is to have the federal government take the initiative in doing things. One field which we have been slowly working is ARDA,-
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the minister in that they have been slowly working that field. We introduced ARDA and had resources development going full steam ahead until this government moved in with its propaganda and gimmick techniques, and tried to substitute those things for economic progress.
In the one minute which remains, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He said:
What constitutes a nation is... having accomplished great things in common in the past and having the wish to accomplish more in the future.
That is what the hon. gentleman said on Wednesday, March 7, before the government even thought of the flag issue as a red herring technique. I agree with him heartily.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten thirty?
A motion to adjourn the house under provisional standing order 39A deemed to have been moved:
FEDERAL SHARE OF WINTER WORKS PROGRAM [Translation]

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon on the orders of the day, I asked a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) with regard to the incentive winter works program set up a few years ago in order to provide assistance, through municipalities, to the great number of unemployed and, by the same token, to their families, during the winter season considered as an off-season for workers.

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I wanted to know if the government had paid its share for all works performed under this program during the 1963-1964 season, because several persons, namely the mayors and secretaries of municipalities in my county, have asked me why they have not yet been paid for those works already completed since April last. Those people enquired from Quebec, and Quebec suggested that the delay was due to Ottawa.
Now, I would like to know whether it is true that the federal government delays the payment for those projects, and for what reason.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that the situation is not peculiar to my constituency, for I find in the newspaper La Frontiere of Thursday, August 20, 1964, on page 10, the following article:
No payment made on $300,000 worth of winter works in Rouyn-Noranda.
Settlers and workmen in twelve parishes of the Rouyn-Noranda county, in which winter works were completed in April last, are still waiting for their pay.
In most parishes, the Rouyn banks financed the major part of the works, so that the workers might receive part of their salaries.
Note this word: part of-
*-their salaries. But the backers of those projects expect that the provincial government will give them the money to reimburse the advances granted by the banks.
According to provincial authorities, five parishes were to be paid on June 15, and seven others on June 20. Now, none of those twelve parishes has yet received any money.
The amounts due by the provincial government, under the federal-provincial agreement on winter works to fight seasonal unemployment, would amount to $300,000 in the county of Rouyn-Noranda only.
Meanwhile, the grocers, butchers, and business people who granted credit to the labourers and settlers, now begin to press them for payment.
As you know, the work has been completed since the end of April.
Those labourers hope to be paid before new winter works begin for 1964-65.
We know that the winter works incentive program was set up to assist those who otherwise could not find a job during the off season. Most of those people have families to support and children at school and besides, they are not free from illness any more than others. They needs money to buy the necessities or obtain the services they need but, in most cases, that joint plan did them more harm than good.
During the last week end, an elector of my riding came to see me to explain the situation he was facing, like those who live in the same community and took part in those works, and that is the case of almost every community in northwestern Quebec.

In the municipality of St. Vital de Clermont, in Abitibi West, work started around December 3, 1963 and ended on April 30, 1964. A first payment was made on June 9, 1964 and the balance has not been paid yet.
Like many others, that municipality could not get credit from the caisse populaire or the banks in La Sarre. Consequently, those people had to work all winter without salary, without income, and some of them had enough stamps to be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. On the other hand, the unemployment insurance offices in Rouyn or Val d'Or refused to pay them benefits since there was work available in their parishes; others who otherwise could have secured help from the social service were refused for the same reason. Go and cut branches or shovel snow.
Now, it happened, Mr. Speaker, that those day labourer settlers went to their general merchant, their supplier, and he was kind and even charitable enough to sell on credit all through the winter, but when the first part of the works was paid on June 9 last, the merchant took everything and kept everything, and we cannot blame him for it.
However, the poor unemployed have nothing yet, as usual. That will have to be changed because there is a class in the twentieth century civilization, in that affluent century of ours, for whom it is always "nothing".
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Minister of Labour and the government to find an arrangement with the province of Quebec and the other provinces so that those who participate in unemployment work will be paid regularly every two weeks. They are like everybody else; they are entitled to the salary they need to support their family.
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will get a satisfactory answer.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) put a question to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen), and though I have not been able to get the exact wording of it, the question appeared to me to be, has the federal government honoured all of its obligations under the 1963-64 municipal winter works incentive program?
The figures that I have been able to obtain are not broken down province by province. However the federal government has approved projects up to $52 million and payments made to the provinces to date amount

to $17,694,000. Claims on hand and in process of payment amount to $5,529,000. Of course the payments are made by the federal government when it has received claims from the provincial governments. I would assume if the province of Quebec is behind in making these claims to the federal government it is in no different situation from the other provinces.
As can be pointed out, only something more than $17 million has been authorized, and the reason the payments have not been made is simply that the claims have not come in as certified; but all claims received since August 7 have been paid.
The federal government makes its contribution only when the province has certified that
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion these undertakings are capable, under the legislation, of receiving the payments. It is regrettable if these employees have not been paid for the work they have done; but though we regret it, it is not within the competence of the federal government to direct these payments. We only make the payments as the claims are received. The department would be very interested in endeavouring to see to it that payments are made as the work is performed but that, of course, would require some further negotiations. I will certainly bring this to the attention of the department again.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.40 p.m.
